### Issue description

Two separate factors make this write slow.

1. **Parallelism is tied to top-level columns.** Splitting the same 32 fields into 4 top-level columns leaves Polars' CPU about the same, but cuts wall time about 3.5×, from 1 core busy to 3.3–3.7. `write_parquet` and `sink_parquet` behave the same way, so a single nested column gets one thread on either path.
2. **The Dremel level walk is slow per value.** On the single column, Polars spends 2.1–2.2 s of CPU against pyarrow's 1.4–1.5 s, and pyarrow's figure includes converting the frame to Arrow. pyarrow encodes column chunks on one thread by default, so this compares one core with one core. Splitting the columns doesn't reduce this cost, so it's separate from factor 1.

Real data stresses factor 2 much harder than the demo, because it's deeper and sparser. This came up writing Wikidata claims: 10,000 rows in one top-level column, with 94 leaf fields under lists up to 5 deep, mostly null.

| Writer | Wall | CPU |
|---|---|---|
| `sink_parquet`, Polars 2.0.0 | 19.7 s | 19.5 s |
| arrow-rs writer (the polars-genson package), one task per leaf column | 0.9 s | 3.3 s |

That's about 6× more CPU per value than arrow-rs.

More detail is in [this write-up](https://github.com/lmmx/polars-genson/blob/f6a6b29/docs/journal/2026-10-21-polars-claims.md).

### Expected behavior

Writing a single nested column should keep all cores busy, as arrow-rs does by encoding each leaf column as its own task. The CPU per value should be comparable to pyarrow's.

#### Root cause (polars-parquet / polars-stream, the 0.55.1 sources behind the Polars 2.0.0 wheel)

1. `polars-stream/.../parquet/row_group_encoder.rs` runs one task per top-level column. Inside that task, all of the column's leaves are encoded one after another (the loop over `array_to_columns(...)`).
2. For each nested leaf, each page walks the leaf's levels from the root three times, each with a fresh `BufferedDremelIter`: `num_values` (`BufferedDremelIter::new(nested).count()`), then `write_rep_levels`, then `write_def_levels`. Each leaf also repeats the walk over the ancestors it shares with its sibling leaves.

Stack samples of the official 2.0.0 wheel writing the Wikidata table put 94% of the busy thread in `BufferedDremelIter::next`:

| Caller | Share of samples |
|---|---|
| `write_def_levels` | 40% |
| the `num_values` count, from the leaf's `array_to_page` | 29% |
| `write_rep_levels` | 26% |
| zstd and conversion | 6% |

The split matches three walks, with the count taking about a third.

#### Possible fixes

- **Encode each leaf as its own task.** `array_to_columns` already returns one independent `Send` page iterator per leaf, so this looks like a scheduling change local to the row-group encoder.
- **Compute count, rep and def levels in one pass** instead of three. This alone should remove about a third of the level-walk time.
- **Compute levels once per column, in ranges,** as arrow-rs's `LevelInfoBuilder` does, instead of per leaf and per element.

### Issue description

Two separate factors make this write slow.

1. **Parallelism is tied to top-level columns.** Splitting the same 32 fields into 4 top-level columns leaves Polars' CPU about the same, but cuts wall time about 3.5×, from 1 core busy to 3.3–3.7. `write_parquet` and `sink_parquet` behave the same way, so a single nested column gets one thread on either path.
2. **The Dremel level walk is slow per value.** On the single column, Polars spends 2.1–2.2 s of CPU against pyarrow's 1.4–1.5 s, and pyarrow's figure includes converting the frame to Arrow. pyarrow encodes column chunks on one thread by default, so this compares one core with one core. Splitting the columns doesn't reduce this cost, so it's separate from factor 1.

Real data stresses factor 2 much harder than the demo, because it's deeper and sparser. This came up writing Wikidata claims: 10,000 rows in one top-level column, with 94 leaf fields under lists up to 5 deep, mostly null.

| Writer | Wall | CPU |
|---|---|---|
| `sink_parquet`, Polars 2.0.0 | 19.7 s | 19.5 s |
| arrow-rs writer (the polars-genson package), one task per leaf column | 0.9 s | 3.3 s |

That's about 6× more CPU per value than arrow-rs.

More detail is in [this write-up](https://github.com/lmmx/polars-genson/blob/f6a6b29/docs/journal/2026-10-21-polars-claims.md).

### Expected behavior

Writing a single nested column should keep all cores busy, as arrow-rs does by encoding each leaf column as its own task. The CPU per value should be comparable to pyarrow's.

#### Root cause (polars-parquet / polars-stream, the 0.55.1 sources behind the Polars 2.0.0 wheel)

1. `polars-stream/.../parquet/row_group_encoder.rs` runs one task per top-level column. Inside that task, all of the column's leaves are encoded one after another (the loop over `array_to_columns(...)`).
2. For each nested leaf, each page walks the leaf's levels from the root three times, each with a fresh `BufferedDremelIter`: `num_values` (`BufferedDremelIter::new(nested).count()`), then `write_rep_levels`, then `write_def_levels`. Each leaf also repeats the walk over the ancestors it shares with its sibling leaves.

Stack samples of the official 2.0.0 wheel writing the Wikidata table put 94% of the busy thread in `BufferedDremelIter::next`:

| Caller | Share of samples |
|---|---|
| `write_def_levels` | 40% |
| the `num_values` count, from the leaf's `array_to_page` | 29% |
| `write_rep_levels` | 26% |
| zstd and conversion | 6% |

The split matches three walks, with the count taking about a third.

#### Possible fixes

- **Encode each leaf as its own task.** `array_to_columns` already returns one independent `Send` page iterator per leaf, so this looks like a scheduling change local to the row-group encoder.
- **Compute count, rep and def levels in one pass** instead of three. This alone should remove about a third of the level-walk time.
- **Compute levels once per column, in ranges,** as arrow-rs's `LevelInfoBuilder` does, instead of per leaf and per element.

### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.

### Reproducible example


```python
import glob, json
from datetime import datetime
import polars as pl

pl.DataFrame({
    "id": [1, 2],
    "ts": [datetime(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 100000), datetime(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 123456)],
}).write_delta("ts_table")

for line in open(glob.glob("ts_table/_delta_log/*.json")[0]):
    if "add" in json.loads(line):
        print(json.loads(line)["add"]["stats"])

for pred in [pl.col("ts") == datetime(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 123456),
             pl.col("ts") > datetime(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 123400)]:
    print(pl.read_delta("ts_table").filter(pred)["id"].to_list(),
          pl.scan_delta("ts_table").filter(pred).collect()["id"].to_list())
```

Output:

```
{"numRecords":2,"minValues":{"ts":"2024-01-01 00:00:00.100","id":1},"maxValues":{"ts":"2024-01-01 00:00:00.123","id":2},"nullCount":{"id":0,"ts":0}}
[2] []
[2] []
```


### Log output

```shell
(POLARS_VERBOSE=1, scan_delta with the filter)
DeltaDataset: to_dataset_scan(): version: None, limit: None, projection: None, filter_columns: ['ts'], statistics_columns: None, use_pyarrow: False
initialize_scan_predicate: Source filter mask initialization via table statistics
initialize_scan_predicate: Predicate pushdown allows skipping 1 / 1 files
apply_scan_predicate_to_scan_ir: PredicateFileSkip { no_residual_predicate: false, original_len: 1 }
```

### Issue description


The Delta protocol says about per-file statistics: "Timestamp columns are truncated down to milliseconds" ([PROTOCOL.md L2686](https://github.com/delta-io/delta/blob/36cc4179881987f7920fd3dea0d15fc62867c4d0/PROTOCOL.md?plain=1#L2686)). The file above holds `00:00:00.123456`, and its `maxValues` records `00:00:00.123`. `scan_delta` takes `maxValues` as an exact upper bound, so it skips the file for any predicate that needs a value above `.123000` (`ts == .123456`, `ts > .1234`), and the matching row is missing from the result. `read_delta(...).filter(...)` returns it. The same happens for `Datetime` columns with a time zone. The table here is written by Polars' own `write_delta` (deltalake writer); the truncation is what the protocol prescribes for every writer.

A common pattern this breaks is incremental reading with `scan_delta(...).filter(pl.col("ts") > last_watermark)`: rows in the last millisecond of a file are skipped.

Cause (main c706e7eb): `_extract_table_statistics_from_delta_add_actions` copies the add actions' `max` values unchanged into the `<col>_max` statistics used for file skipping ([`py-polars/src/polars/io/delta/_utils.py` L176-L185](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/c706e7ebe8b6422679b37e46fbe6026cb46a9a7c/py-polars/src/polars/io/delta/_utils.py#L176-L185)), called from [`_dataset.py` L210-L217](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/c706e7ebe8b6422679b37e46fbe6026cb46a9a7c/py-polars/src/polars/io/delta/_dataset.py#L210-L217). For `Datetime` columns (including struct fields) with a unit finer than milliseconds, the max should be widened by 1 ms minus one unit (or the statistic not used). The min is truncated down, so it stays a valid lower bound.

Same output on main c706e7ebe8b6422679b37e46fbe6026cb46a9a7c (2026-10-18, built from source) and the 2.0.0 wheel from PyPI, both with deltalake 1.6.6.


### Expected behavior

`[2] [2]` for both predicates: `scan_delta(...).filter(...)` should return the same rows as `read_delta(...).filter(...)`.

### Issue description

Slicing the literal string `"xh"` with `pl.col("c0")` as the start offset and a literal length of 1 succeeds with CPU collection but fails when the same lazy query is collected with `pl.GPUEngine(raise_on_fail=True)`. The input contains a single offset value, `0`.

CPU collection returns a String column `c1` containing `"x"`. GPU collection instead raises `polars.exceptions.ComputeError` wrapping a `NotImplementedError`, with the diagnostic `Slice only supports literal start and stop values`.

This example isolates the GPU limitation for a column-based string-slice offset under strict GPU execution. The length is a literal; the start offset is a column expression.

### Expected behavior

The GPU execution path should support the column-based string-slice offset and return the same schema and value as CPU collection. Slicing `"xh"` from offset 0 with length 1 should produce `"x"`:

```text
shape: (1, 1)
┌─────┐
│ c1  │
│ --- │
│ str │
╞═════╡
│ x   │
└─────┘
```

### Description

Hi,

there is a new driver developed by Microsoft [mssql-python](https://github.com/microsoft/mssql-python)
that supports fetching from the cursor in Apache Arrow format.
Recent SQLAlchemy 2.1 release added support for the mssql-python driver (`mssql+mssqlpython://` url).

`polars.read_database` already has support for SQLAlchemy drivers that support this kind of optimization,
it sniffs the driver name from the `sqlalchemy.Engine` object and uses the optimized Arrow methods if available,
for example for the `oracle+oracledb://` driver.

It seems very natural to extend this support to the new `mssql+mssqlpython://` driver.

### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import io
import pickle
import tempfile
import warnings

import polars as pl
from deltalake import DeltaTable

path = tempfile.mkdtemp()
pl.DataFrame({"a": [0]}).write_delta(path)
pl.DataFrame({"a": [1]}).write_delta(path, mode="append")

lf = pl.scan_delta(DeltaTable(path, version=0))
print(lf.collect()["a"].to_list())
print(pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(lf)).collect()["a"].to_list())
print(pl.LazyFrame.deserialize(io.BytesIO(lf.serialize())).collect()["a"].to_list())

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    lf2 = pl.scan_delta(DeltaTable(path), version=0)
    print(lf2.collect()["a"].to_list(), len(w))
print(pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(lf2)).collect()["a"].to_list())
```

Output on main (18611065d9, built from source) with deltalake 1.6.6:

```
[0]
[1, 0]
[1, 0]
[1, 0] 0
[0]
```

Output with polars 1.37.1:

```
[0]
[0]
[0]
[1, 0] 1
[1, 0]
```

### Issue description

Since #26190 (1.38), `scan_delta` keeps a `DeltaTable` source in a `NoPickleOption` with `version=None`. After pickling or `serialize()`, the dataset reloads the table from its URI at `version=None`, i.e. the latest version, and returns different rows without an error.

Also, `version=` given with a `DeltaTable` source is ignored without the `RuntimeWarning` ("When supplying a DeltaTable directly, `version`, `storage_options`, and `delta_table_options` are ignored") that 1.37 emitted. It is only applied after pickling, when the table is reloaded from its URI, so the same LazyFrame returns the latest version locally (`[1, 0]`) and version 0 after a round trip (`[0]`).

### Expected behavior

A LazyFrame returns the same rows before and after pickling/`serialize()`: the `DeltaTable`'s loaded version (`[0]` in the first case), e.g. by recording `table.version()` in the dataset when a `DeltaTable` is passed. `version=` with a `DeltaTable` source warns again (or raises).

body_text:
### Checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of Polars.

### Reproducible example

```python
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "arr": [[1, 2], [3]]})
df.sql("SELECT id, a, b FROM self CROSS JOIN UNNEST(arr, arr) AS u(a, b)")
```

### Log output

```shell
thread '<unnamed>' panicked at crates/polars-plan/src/plans/conversion/dsl_to_ir/mod.rs:1342:87:
called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value
...
pyo3_runtime.PanicException: called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value
```

### Issue description

A lateral `UNNEST` that names the same column twice panics. With two different columns (`UNNEST(arr, arr2)`) it works.

The SQL side calls `rename(["arr", "arr"], ["a", "b"], strict=true)`. The rename conversion in `dsl_to_ir` dedups the old names, so `arr` is replaced once (to `a`; `b` is lost). Its strict check then sees 1 replacement for 2 names, assumes a column is missing, searches for one, finds none, and unwraps `None`.

### Expected behavior

Each output column gets its own copy, as in Postgres:

```
 id | a | b
----+---+---
  1 | 1 | 1
  1 | 2 | 2
  2 | 3 | 3
```

Note, some engines raise on duplicate names in UNNEST (e.g., duckdb).

A duplicate name in a strict rename should also raise an error rather than panic.

### Installed versions

Polars 2.0.0 (PyPI, build 22a147de3d), Python 3.13.5, Linux x86_64. Also on main (18611065d9).

A scoped custom element registry can be attached to a document, shadow root, and elements.

When creating elements with `createElementNS`, you need to pass in the custom element registry you want to use, otherwise it defaults to the document's registry:

```js
document.createElementNS(nameSpace, tagName, {
  customElementRegistry,
});
```

If the developer is rendering into a shadow root, Preact will currently create all elements using the document's `customElementRegistry`, rather than the shadow root's.

Some ways around this:

Preact looks up the `customElementRegistry` of the rendered root, and uses that in its calls to `createElementNS`.

Or, an option to `render` allows the developer to provide a `customElementRegistry` when creating elements.

Or, Preact provides a hook to override how `createElementNS` is called.

There is a typo in the mathematical formulas used to determine the probability of flipping a bit during the randomized merge in `SfmSketch`, which results in too many 1-bits in the sketch. This results in sketches that appear to have more elements than they should (i.e., an upward bias in cardinality).

The bug is present in both Java and Velox. A fix for Velox is available at https://github.com/facebookincubator/velox/pull/18790.

## Your Environment

n/a

## Expected Behavior

Merging two noisy sketches should result in a sketch that is distributionally equivalent to the sketch of their union, but with higher noise.

## Current Behavior

The merged sketch has excessive 1-bits due to a typo in the formula, resulting in upward bias in cardinality estimation that is particularly notable at epsilon <= 1.

## Possible Solution

See fix in https://github.com/facebookincubator/velox/pull/18790.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create two noisy SFM sketches with, e.g., epsilon=1.
2. Merge them together.
3. Estimate cardinality.
4. On average, this will overshoot the true cardinality of the set union.

## Screenshots (if appropriate)

n/a

## Context

Fixed in Velox: https://github.com/facebookincubator/velox/pull/18790

## Summary

`UnaliasSymbolReferences` optimizer enters an infinite loop (or OOM) when processing a query that causes the symbol `mapping` to contain a cycle. The root cause is the deduplication logic in `canonicalize(Assignments)`, which merges different symbols that fold to *equal* `ConstantExpression` values. Because `ConstantExpression.equals()/hashCode()` is value-based, distinct columns filtered to the same literal via `IN('...')` become "equal" and get mapped to each other. Across multiple `ProjectNode`s the mappings form a 2-node cycle (A→B, B→A), causing the `while` loop in `canonicalize(VariableReferenceExpression)` to spin forever.

## Affected Version

Reproduced on presto-0.296.

## Steps to Reproduce

### 1. Create the table

```sql
CREATE TABLE ads.ads_bi_tob_exp_app_mall_pool_1d_d_s0(
  `exp_salt` string,
  `exp_layer_id` string,
  `exp_id` string,
  `exp_layer_name` string,
  `exp_name` string,
  `mall_pool_id` string,
  `mall_tag` string,
  `mall_tag_value` string,
  `is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct` string,
  `is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct` string,
  `buk_cnt` double,
  `ad_bill_spend_1d_buk` double,
  `mall_pool_type` string,
  `est_use_amt_buck` bigint,
  `abflag` bigint,
  `est_use_amt` double
)
PARTITIONED BY (`pt` string)
STORED AS ORC;
```

> Only the columns referenced by the reproducer SQL are included above. The original table has 81 columns; the extra columns are irrelevant to the bug.

### 2. Run the reproducer query
**It must be this SQL statement. Reproducing this bug requires extremely strict conditions.**


```sql
SELECT `col_1`,`col_2`,`col_3`,`col_4`,`col_5`,`col_6`,`col_7`,`col_8`,`col_9`,`col_10`,`col_11`,`col_12`,`col_13`
FROM (
  WITH tmp_exp AS
  (
    SELECT
        pt,
        exp_layer_name,
        exp_name,
        abflag,
        is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct,
        is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct,
        mall_tag,
        mall_tag_value,
        mall_pool_id,
        mall_pool_type,
        sum(buk_cnt) AS buk_cnt,
        sum(ad_bill_spend_1d_buk*buk_cnt)/sum(buk_cnt) AS ad_bill_spend_1d_buk,
        nvl(sum(nvl(est_use_amt,est_use_amt_buck)*buk_cnt)/sum(buk_cnt),0.0) AS est_use_amt
    FROM ads.ads_bi_tob_exp_app_mall_pool_1d_d_s0
    WHERE pt BETWEEN '2026-09-07' AND '2026-09-09'
      AND exp_layer_name IN ('goods_subsidy_popup_full')
      AND is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct IN ('ALL')
      AND is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct IN ('ALL')
      AND mall_pool_id IN ('200056')
      AND mall_pool_type IN ('cumulative_pool')
      AND mall_tag IN ('ALL')
      AND mall_tag_value IN ('ALL')
      AND exp_name IN ('GoodsSubsidyPopupFull1')
    GROUP BY
      pt, exp_layer_name, exp_name, abflag,
      is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct,
      is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct,
      mall_tag, mall_tag_value, mall_pool_id, mall_pool_type
  ),
  tmp_base AS
  (
    SELECT
        pt,
        exp_layer_name,
        exp_name,
        abflag,
        is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct,
        is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct,
        mall_tag,
        mall_tag_value,
        mall_pool_id,
        mall_pool_type,
        sum(buk_cnt) AS buk_cnt,
        sum(ad_bill_spend_1d_buk*buk_cnt)/sum(buk_cnt) AS ad_bill_spend_1d_buk,
        nvl(sum(nvl(est_use_amt,est_use_amt_buck)*buk_cnt)/sum(buk_cnt),0.0) AS est_use_amt
    FROM ads.ads_bi_tob_exp_app_mall_pool_1d_d_s0
    WHERE pt BETWEEN '2026-09-07' AND '2026-09-09'
      AND exp_layer_name IN ('goods_subsidy_popup_full')
      AND is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct IN ('ALL')
      AND is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct IN ('ALL')
      AND mall_pool_id IN ('200056')
      AND mall_pool_type IN ('cumulative_pool')
      AND mall_tag IN ('ALL')
      AND mall_tag_value IN ('ALL')
      AND exp_name IN ('goods_subsidy_popup_full_base')
    GROUP BY
      pt, exp_layer_name, exp_name, abflag,
      is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct,
      is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct,

## Root Cause

### The dedup logic in `canonicalize(Assignments)`

`UnaliasSymbolReferences.canonicalize(Assignments)` has a dedup optimization: within a single `ProjectNode`, if two different keys map to the **same deterministic expression**, they are merged into one symbol:

```java
// UnaliasSymbolReferences.java, canonicalize(Assignments)
else if (!isNull(expression) && determinismEvaluator.isDeterministic(expression)) {
    VariableReferenceExpression computedVariable = computedExpressions.get(expression);
    if (computedVariable == null) {
        computedExpressions.put(expression, entry.getKey());
    } else {
        map(entry.getKey(), computedVariable);  // merge: key -> computedVariable
    }
}
```

`computedExpressions` is a `HashMap<RowExpression, VariableReferenceExpression>`. The problem is that `ConstantExpression.equals()/hashCode()` is **value-based**:

```java
// ConstantExpression.java
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(value, type);
}
public boolean equals(Object obj) {
    ...
    return Objects.equals(this.value, other.value)
        && Objects.equals(this.type, other.type);
}
```

For `VARCHAR` type, `value` is a `Slice` (byte buffer), and `Slice.equals` compares byte content. So two `ConstantExpression('ALL', VARCHAR)` from **different columns** are `equals == true` with the same `hashCode`, even though they represent semantically distinct grouping dimensions.

### How the cycle forms

Four columns (`is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct`, `is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct`, `mall_tag`, `mall_tag_value`) are filtered to the same single value `'ALL'` via `IN('ALL')`. After constant folding, they all become `ConstantExpression('ALL', VARCHAR)`.

By adding per-`ProjectNode` debug logging, the cycle formation was traced:

**ProjectNode #3** (columns appear in order A, B, mall_tag, mall_tag_value):
```
key='is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct'  expr=ConstantExpression('ALL')  ← first seen, record
key='is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct'        expr=ConstantExpression('ALL')  ← equals hit!
  → map('is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct' → 'is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct')   i.e. B→A
key='mall_tag'                                  expr=ConstantExpression('ALL')  ← equals hit!
  → map('mall_tag' → 'is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct')
key='mall_tag_value'                            expr=ConstantExpression('ALL')  ← equals hit!
  → map('mall_tag_value' → 'is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct')
```

**ProjectNode #9** (same constants, but in order B, A):
```
key='is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct'        expr=ConstantExpression('ALL')  ← first seen, record
key='is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct'  expr=ConstantExpression('ALL')  ← equals hit!
  → map('is_mall_online_ad_goods_cnt_above_99pct' → 'is_mall_ad_bill_spend_above_99pct')  i.e. A→B  ← CYCLE!
```

ProjectNode #3 establishes B→A, ProjectNode #9 establishes A→B — a 2-node cycle.

The `while` loop in `canonicalize(VariableReferenceExpression)` then spins forever:

```java
private VariableReferenceExpression canonicalize(VariableReferenceExpression variable)
{
    String canonical = variable.getName();
    while (mapping.containsKey(canonical)) {  // ← A↔B cycle, infinite loop
        canonical = mapping.get(canonical);
    }
    ...
}
```

### Why this is a bug (not just a missing cycle guard)

The dedup optimization assumes "identical deterministic expressions can be merged into one symbol." This assumption is **wrong** for `GROUPING SETS` — the grouping dimension columns are semantically distinct even if their values happen to be identical. Merging them breaks the grouping semantics.

### Why the reproducer cannot be trivially small

The bug does not depend on SQL topology alone — it depends on **plan depth**. With a small SQL, the constant is folded once at the CTE entry and reused as a single symbol across all downstream `ProjectNode`s, so dedup never triggers. Only when the plan is deep enough (CTE + derived column layer + join + grouping sets + a complex aggregate expression that references both a derived column and a raw column) does the optimizer fold the constant **independently** in multiple `ProjectNode`s, producing multiple `ConstantExpression('ALL')` instances that are `equals` but come from different columns.

## Proposed Fix

Two-layer guard in `UnaliasSymbolReferences.java`:

### 1. Cycle detection in `map()` (primary fix)

Before establishing `variable → canonical`, check whether `canonical` already (transitively) maps back to `variable`. If so, skip the mapping to keep both symbols independent:

```java
private void map(VariableReferenceExpression variable, VariableReferenceExpression canonical)
{
    Preconditions.checkArgument(!variable.equals(canonical), "Can't map variable to itself: %s", variable);
    String variableName = variable.getName();
    String canonicalName = canonical.getName();
    if (wouldCreateCycle(variableName, canonicalName)) {
        return;
    }
    mapping.put(variableName, canonicalName);
}

private boolean wouldCreateCycle(String from, String to)
{
    String current = to;
    while (mapping.containsKey(current)) {
        current = mapping.get(current);
        if (current.equals(from)) {
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}
```

Skipping the mapping is safe: a cycle means the two symbols are being merged into each other via different paths. Keeping them independent does not lose any information — the dedup optimization is an optimization, not a correctness requirement.

### 2. Hop limit in `canonicalize(VariableReferenceExpression)` (defensive guard)

```java
private VariableReferenceExpression canonicalize(VariableReferenceExpression variable)
{
    String canonical = variable.getName();
    int hops = 0;
    while (mapping.containsKey(canonical)) {
        canonical = mapping.get(canonical);
        if (++hops > mapping.size()) {
            break;  // cycle detected, avoid infinite loop
        }
    }
    return new VariableReferenceExpression(variable.getSourceLocation(), canonical,
        types.get(new SymbolReference(getNodeLocation(variable.getSourceLocation()), canonical)));
}
```

Before establishing `variable → canonical`, check whether `canonical` already (transitively) maps back to `variable`. If so, skip the mapping to keep both symbols independent:

```java
private void map(VariableReferenceExpression variable, VariableReferenceExpression canonical)
{
    Preconditions.checkArgument(!variable.equals(canonical), "Can't map variable to itself: %s", variable);
    String variableName = variable.getName();
    String canonicalName = canonical.getName();
    if (wouldCreateCycle(variableName, canonicalName)) {
        return;
    }
    mapping.put(variableName, canonicalName);
}

private boolean wouldCreateCycle(String from, String to)
{
    String current = to;
    while (mapping.containsKey(current)) {
        current = mapping.get(current);
        if (current.equals(from)) {
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}
```

Skipping the mapping is safe: a cycle means the two symbols are being merged into each other via different paths. Keeping them independent does not lose any information — the dedup optimization is an optimization, not a correctness requirement.

### 2. Hop limit in `canonicalize(VariableReferenceExpression)` (defensive guard)

```java
private VariableReferenceExpression canonicalize(VariableReferenceExpression variable)
{
    String canonical = variable.getName();
    int hops = 0;
    while (mapping.containsKey(canonical)) {
        canonical = mapping.get(canonical);
        if (++hops > mapping.size()) {
            break;  // cycle detected, avoid infinite loop
        }
    }
    return new VariableReferenceExpression(variable.getSourceLocation(), canonical,
        types.get(new SymbolReference(getNodeLocation(variable.getSourceLocation()), canonical)));
}
```

|----------|-----------|-----------|
| Reproducer SQL (108 lines) | Timeout / OOM | Success (~1s) |
| Original production SQL (385 lines) | Timeout (130s) | Success (2.7s) |
| `TestUnaliasSymbolReferences` unit tests | — | 6/6 passed |

For a join shaped like

```sql
SELECT ...
FROM a JOIN b ON k1 = k2 AND IF(v1 = v2, TRUE, FALSE)
WHERE p(x, y, z);
```

the resulting INNER join filter evaluates the post-join predicate `p(x, y, z)` (pushed down from the WHERE clause) **before** the ON-clause equality `IF(v1 = v2, TRUE, FALSE)`.

Expected: cheap equalities from the ON clause run first, and `p(x, y, z)` runs after everything else. Join filters short-circuit left to right, so burying a selective equality behind an expensive pushed-down expression wastes per-pair CPU in the join.

Mechanism: `PredicatePushDown.processInnerJoin` appends the inherited post-join conjuncts to the join filter ahead of the original ON-clause non-equi conjuncts, and nothing re-orders the merged filter by cost/selectivity afterwards.

## Your Environment
* Presto version used: master at 9d4e69dce4 ("refactor: Declare a signature when registering a test RPC function (#28496)")
* Storage (HDFS/S3/GCS..): local file system
* Data source and connector used: Iceberg connector (Java reader), Hive and Hadoop catalogs
* Deployment (Cloud or On-prem): local `DistributedQueryRunner` in tests

## Expected Behavior

After a field inside a struct column is renamed, reading that field by its new name returns the values already written, just like a renamed top-level column does.

## Current Behavior

The renamed field comes back as NULL for data files written before the rename. The data is still in the files. It is read by the old name and not found.

How bad it is depends on the file format:

| Query (after renaming `s.a` to `s.a_renamed`) | Parquet | Parquet, `parquet_dereference_pushdown_enabled = false` | ORC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SELECT s` | `{a_renamed=10, b=20}` ✅ | `{a_renamed=10, b=20}` ✅ | `{a_renamed=NULL, b=20}` ❌ |
| `SELECT s.a_renamed` | `NULL` ❌ | `10` ✅ | `NULL` ❌ |
| `SELECT count(*) WHERE s.a_renamed = 10` | `1` ✅ | `1` ✅ | `0` ❌ |

The field `b`, which was not renamed, is always read correctly. The result is the same with `pushdown_subfields_enabled` on or off.

## Possible Solution

Iceberg matches columns by field id, not by name, so that a rename does not need to rewrite any data. The Presto Iceberg reader does this for top-level columns, but not always for fields inside a struct:

* **Parquet:** a top-level column is found by field id ([`IcebergPageSourceProvider.java:466`](https://github.com/prestodb/presto/blob/9d4e69dce4770b44a460776db4ace2a95d616d45/presto-iceberg/src/main/java/com/facebook/presto/iceberg/IcebergPageSourceProvider.java#L466)). A dereference pushed down into the Parquet reader, such as `s.a_renamed`, is found by its name path instead ([`IcebergPageSourceProvider.java:459`](https://github.com/prestodb/presto/blob/9d4e69dce4770b44a460776db4ace2a95d616d45/presto-iceberg/src/main/java/com/facebook/presto/iceberg/IcebergPageSourceProvider.java#L459)). The file only has a field named `a`, so nothing is found and NULL is returned.
* **ORC:** even a full read of the struct loses the renamed field, so fields inside a struct seem to be matched by name in the ORC path as well. I haven't looked into where yet.

Workaround for Parquet: `SET SESSION iceberg.parquet_dereference_pushdown_enabled = false`. I found no workaround for ORC.

## Steps to Reproduce

Presto can't rename a nested field (`ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` only works on top-level columns), so the rename has to be done through the Iceberg API, Spark, or another engine.

1. In Presto:
   ```sql
   CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, s ROW(a INTEGER, b INTEGER)) WITH (format = 'ORC');  -- or 'PARQUET'
   INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, ROW(10, 20));
   ```
2. Rename the nested field through Iceberg, for example in a Java test:
   ```java
   table.updateSchema().renameColumn("s.a", "a_renamed").commit();
   ```
   or in Spark: `ALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN s.a TO a_renamed`.
3. In Presto:
   ```sql
   SELECT s FROM t;                                  -- ORC: a_renamed is NULL
   SELECT s.a_renamed, s.b FROM t;                   -- NULL, 20 (both formats)
   SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE s.a_renamed = 10;    -- ORC: 0
   ```
   Expected: `10` for `s.a_renamed` everywhere, and a count of `1`.

## Context

I found this while adding a test for time travel reads over nested schema changes in #28503. That PR doesn't touch this code path, and the results above are from master without it. Tables whose nested fields are renamed by Spark or another engine will return NULLs in Presto for rows written before the rename, with no error.

* **Parquet:** a top-level column is found by field id ([`IcebergPageSourceProvider.java:466`](https://github.com/prestodb/presto/blob/9d4e69dce4770b44a460776db4ace2a95d616d45/presto-iceberg/src/main/java/com/facebook/presto/iceberg/IcebergPageSourceProvider.java#L466)). A dereference pushed down into the Parquet reader, such as `s.a_renamed`, is found by its name path instead ([`IcebergPageSourceProvider.java:459`](https://github.com/prestodb/presto/blob/9d4e69dce4770b44a460776db4ace2a95d616d45/presto-iceberg/src/main/java/com/facebook/presto/iceberg/IcebergPageSourceProvider.java#L459)). The file only has a field named `a`, so nothing is found and NULL is returned.
* **ORC:** even a full read of the struct loses the renamed field, so fields inside a struct seem to be matched by name in the ORC path as well. I haven't looked into where yet.

Workaround for Parquet: `SET SESSION iceberg.parquet_dereference_pushdown_enabled = false`. I found no workaround for ORC.

## Steps to Reproduce

Presto can't rename a nested field (`ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` only works on top-level columns), so the rename has to be done through the Iceberg API, Spark, or another engine.

1. In Presto:
   ```sql
   CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, s ROW(a INTEGER, b INTEGER)) WITH (format = 'ORC');  -- or 'PARQUET'
   INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, ROW(10, 20));
   ```
2. Rename the nested field through Iceberg, for example in a Java test:
   ```java
   table.updateSchema().renameColumn("s.a", "a_renamed").commit();
   ```
   or in Spark: `ALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN s.a TO a_renamed`.
3. In Presto:
   ```sql
   SELECT s FROM t;                                  -- ORC: a_renamed is NULL
   SELECT s.a_renamed, s.b FROM t;                   -- NULL, 20 (both formats)
   SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE s.a_renamed = 10;    -- ORC: 0
   ```
   Expected: `10` for `s.a_renamed` everywhere, and a count of `1`.

## Context

I found this while adding a test for time travel reads over nested schema changes in #28503. That PR doesn't touch this code path, and the results above are from master without it. Tables whose nested fields are renamed by Spark or another engine will return NULLs in Presto for rows written before the rename, with no error.

<!--- Provide a general summary of the issue in the Title above -->
<!--- Look through existing open and closed issues to see if someone has reported the issue before -->

## Your Environment
* Presto version used: 0.301-SNAPSHOT
* Storage (HDFS/S3/GCS..): Local file system (reproduced locally and in GitHub Actions CI); the issue is in file-format handling, so it is not storage specific
* Data source and connector used: Iceberg connector on Presto C++ (Prestissimo) native workers, table `format = 'ORC'`
* Deployment (Cloud or On-prem): Local native query runner (`presto-native-tests`) and CI

## Expected Behavior
A native worker can read the Iceberg ORC table data it wrote itself. `SELECT` after `INSERT` should return the inserted rows, as it does for PARQUET tables and for ORC tables written by the Java worker.

## Current Behavior
Reading any data file written by the native worker for an Iceberg `ORC` table fails while parsing the file footer:

Unpartitioned table:
```
    VeloxException: [Range Constraint Violation: -6 >= 0]: lz4 failed to decompress. Info: File Footer
    Split Hive: file:/.../data/485bc7cd-75f3-47bd-879f-57a78af00023.dwrf 0 - 869
      at velox::dwio::common::compression::Lz4Decompressor::decompressInternal
      at velox::dwio::common::compression::PagedInputStream::readOrSkip
      at velox::dwrf::ReaderBase::ReaderBase
      at velox::dwrf::DwrfReader::create
      at velox::orc::OrcReaderFactory::createReader
      at velox::connector::hive::iceberg::IcebergSplitReader::prepareSplit
```
Identity-partitioned table:
```
    VeloxRuntimeError: impl->ParseFromZeroCopyStream(input)
    Split Hive: file:/.../data/0f234d27-a0f9-473b-8ce0-e5c4eb51a2cb.dwrf 0 - 669
      at velox::dwrf::ReaderBase::ReaderBase
      at velox::orc::OrcReaderFactory::createReader
```

The failure happens for the very first file written, so it does not depend on schema evolution, defaults, partitioning or filter pushdown.

## Possible Solution
<!--- Not obligatory, but suggest a fix/reason for the bug or a workaround -->

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Start a Presto cluster with native (Prestissimo) workers and the Iceberg connector, or use `PrestoNativeQueryRunnerUtils.nativeIcebergQueryRunnerBuilder()`.
2. `CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, name VARCHAR) WITH (format = 'ORC');`
3. `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'Alice'), (2, 'Bob');`
4. `SELECT * FROM t;` - fails with `lz4 failed to decompress ... File Footer`.

(With `partitioning = ARRAY['name']` in step 2, step 4 fails with `ParseFromZeroCopyStream(input)` instead.)

## Screenshots (if appropriate)
N/A

## Context
Found while adding Iceberg V3 `write-default` support for native workers (PR #28565). A reviewer asked to port the Java `TestIcebergV3.testInsertWithPartitionEvolution` cases, which run with both PARQUET and ORC. All PARQUET runs pass, and all ORC runs fail on this footer issue, which is unrelated to write-default.

Existing native ORC suites (`TestPrestoNativeIcebergTpchQueriesOrcUsingThrift`, `TestPrestoNativeIcebergPositionDeleteQueriesOrcUsingThrift`) don't catch this because their data is written by the Java worker (genuine ORC) and only read by the native worker. No current test has the native worker both write and read Iceberg ORC.

ORC is excluded from `TestIcebergV3DefaultColumnValues.withPartitioningProvider()` with a TODO until this is fixed. Any user writing Iceberg ORC tables through native workers will hit this on read.

body_text:
When using the testing Presto server with multiple JDBC-based connectors, the serialized handles can contain incorrect type information. For example, a serialized `mysql` table layout handle might look like
```
{
  "@type" : "postgresql",
  "layoutString" : "{domains=ALL, additionalPredicate={}}",
  "table" : {
    "@type" : "postgresql",
    "catalogName" : "tpch",
    "connectorId" : "mysql",
    "schemaTableName" : {
      "schema" : "tpch",
      "table" : "lineitem"
    },
    "tableName" : "lineitem"
  },
  "tupleDomain" : {
    "columnDomains" : [ ]
  }
}
```

here the `@type` is incorrectly set to the wrong connector name `postgresql`.

This was discovered in the `FlightShim::TestArrowFederationNativeQueriesMixedConnectors` tests where multiple JDBC-based connectors are all installed directly to the Presto server.

This is happening because when the coordinator serializes the connector handles, the first serializer that matches the instance of the handle is used as the type. Since all the connectors use the same JDBC-based handles, the incorrect connector type is used.

body_text: Environment Presto 0.281 (internally built from ~0.281, Java 8, G1) ~80 workers across 2 availability zones; issue happens on a single worker at a time Default compiler.expression-cache-size (10,000) Symptom Periodically, a single worker gets "stuck": The blocked-thread count keeps climbing (~115 → 156 over the ~40s window I sampled) and never recovers on its own. Queries scheduled on that worker fail with timeouts; other queries are unaffected until the coordinator routes around it. CPU flame graphs can't even be captured during the episode (async-profiler struggles), so I set up jstack sampling every 5s instead. Restarting the worker restores normal operation. I captured 5 jstack dumps (one every ~5–10s) during an episode. Summary: Key observations: No deadlock detected (Found one Java-level deadlock absent in all dumps). ~30–40 threads are concurrently RUNNABLE in native class-definition/initialization paths, all from expression codegen: ClassLoader.defineClass1 (Native Method) → DynamicClassLoader.defineClass / defineClasses → CompilerUtils.defineClass → PageFunctionCompiler.compileProjectionInternal (PageFunctionCompiler.java:338) → ExpressionCompiler.compilePageProcessor → LocalExecutionPlanner.plan (visitProject / visitAggregation) → SqlTaskExecutionFactory.create (SqlTaskExecutionFactory.java:104) → SqlTask.updateTask (SqlTask.java:459) <- synchronized (SqlTask) → SqlTaskManager.updateTask → TaskResource.createOrUpdateTask (HTTP) Another 16 threads are in Class.getDeclaredConstructors0 via Reflection.constructorMethodHandle (first reflective access to the freshly generated class, still inside the same compile path), and 11 in Reflection.initialize (). All of this happens inside the SqlTask monitor (SqlTask.updateTask is synchronized, and it calls SqlTaskExecutionFactory.create → LocalExecutionPlanner.plan on the calling thread). While one thread compiles, other HTTP requests for the same task block on the same monitor (SqlTask.updateTask line 449). Jetty http-worker threads get consumed one by one — each is renamed to Task- while it runs planning/compilation, and they don't get returned fast enough. As the blocked count grows, the HTTP pool (default 200) drains and task updates from the coordinator start timing out, which is what eventually fails queries. At the moment of the episode, 50+ distinct queries were actively being planned on this worker, with creation timestamps heavily concentrated within the same minute (e.g., ~20 queries created within a 60s window all landing tasks on this worker). So this looks like a burst of new-query task updates hitting the worker simultaneously, most of them missing the expression cache on first compile. Separately, split-runner threads (worker task-processor-* pool, 36 threads) block on DriverFactory.createDriver (synchronized) while a driver is being created for the same pipeline — the DriverFactory lock is held while operator factories instantiate, which indirectly waits on the compile results. This couples the execution pool to the compile storm too. Questions Has anyone seen this failure mode — worker-wide thread exhaustion caused by concurrent expression compilation under the SqlTask monitor during a query burst? Is holding LocalExecutionPlanner.plan (including bytecode compilation) inside synchronized(SqlTask.updateTask) intentional, or is there a known reason it can't be moved out of the monitor / done before acquiring the lock? Would it make sense to (a) throttle node-level concurrent expression compilation (semaphore around PageFunctionCompiler), or (b) bound the number of concurrent task plannings per worker? Any prior discussion or PRs on this? Any recommended config/flags to mitigate in the short term (Jetty thread pool sizing, task update retry behavior from the coordinator, etc.) before a code-level fix?

**Prettier 3.8.0**
[Playground link](https://prettier.io/playground/#)
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```sh
--parser typescript
```

**Input:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
class A extends ({}).Foo {}
```

**Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
class A extends {}.Foo {}

```

**Second Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
SyntaxError: Declaration or statement expected. (1:19)
> 1 | class A extends {}.Foo {}
    |                   ^
  2 |
```

**Expected output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
class A extends ({}).Foo {}
```

Or


```tsx
class A extends ({}.Foo) {}
```

**Why?**

TypeScript can't parse it, even for other parsers that can correctly parse, it still confusing.

This looks like a class property access 

```js
class A extends {
  Foo
}.Foo

{}
```

body_text:
In some cases, `prettier` inserts a line break after `=` or `:`, even when the right-hand side is just a single simple expression, such as a long string literal or a function call.

However, from a readability perspective, this kind of line break does not seem to provide much benefit here, and instead makes the code feel visually looser. In particular, inside object literals, it weakens the visual connection between a property and its value, which makes the structure a bit harder to scan.

I know one of the reasons Prettier exists is to stop formatting debates, but this really feels incredibly user-unfriendly to me.

### Input

```ts
const short = 'short'

const long = 'loooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong'

const obj = {
  short: 'short',
  longStr: 'loooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong',
  longCall: looooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong(),
}
```

### Current output

```ts
const short = 'short'

const long =
  'loooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong'

const obj = {
  short: 'short',
  longStr:
    'loooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong',
  longCall:
    looooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong(),
}
```

### Expected output

```ts
const short = 'short'

const long = 'loooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong'

const obj = {
  short: 'short',
  longStr: 'loooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong',
  longCall: looooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooong(),
}
```

### Why the current behavior feels suboptimal

- The right-hand side is still just a single simple expression.
- Breaking after `=` / `:` makes the visual structure feel looser.
- The added indentation does not seem to provide a clear readability benefit here.
- In object literals especially, the connection between properties and values becomes less direct and harder to scan.

### Suggestion

If the right-hand side is just a single simple expression, would it make sense to prefer keeping it on the same line instead of breaking after `=` / `:`?

If the current behavior is intentional, I’d also be happy to understand the reasoning behind it.

**Input:**

let o = 1;
(
    1 ||
    12345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890
) ?
    2
:   3

```

**Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```jsx
let o = 1
(
    1 ||
    12345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890
) ?
    2
:   3

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```jsx
let o = 1
;(
    1 ||
    12345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890
) ?
    2
:   3
```

**Why?**
The output Prettier gives visibly changes the program, so that it tries to call `1` as a function, instead of assigning it to `o`. I expect that Prettier should maintain the runtime behavior of the code by inserting a semicolon before the parenthesized ternary condition.

**Prettier 3.9.6**

[Playground link](https://prettier.io/playground/#%7B%22content%22%3A%22**a%20_**b**_%20c**%22%2C%22options%22%3A%7B%22parser%22%3A%22markdown%22%7D%7D)

```sh
--parser markdown
```

**Input:**

```markdown
**a _**b**_ c**
```

**Output:**

```markdown
**a _**b**\_ c**
```

**Expected output:**

```markdown
**a _**b**_ c**
```

**Why?**

Prettier itself produces this input when formatting `**a ***b*** c**`. That first pass preserves CommonMark rendering. Formatting again removes the emphasis on `b` and introduces literal underscores. Equivalent formatting that preserves the original emphasis is fine.

Also reproduced on development commit `891accaaab6dab0fbb5eba6748fbb1f5ac4809b5`. Related #17143 changed delimiter styling; this example still fails in 3.9.6.

**Prettier 3.9.9**

### Example 1
[Playground link](https://prettier.io/playground/#N4Igxg9gdgLgprEAuECCuBbABAMSwenyzAB0pgsBBLAXzJABoQIAHGAS2gGdlQWBDAE5c4g5CBgBPFnC5hB7NiBo0gA)

```sh
--parser typescript
```

**Input:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
enum F // c
{ A }
```

**Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
enum F { // c
  A,
}
```

**Second Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
enum F {
  // c
  A,
}
```

### Example 2
[Playground link](https://prettier.io/playground/#N4Igxg9gdgLgprEAuEUCGBbOBnADmsOAAgDEiB6cosAHSmCLQG4iBfOkAGhAlxgEto2ZKHwAnbHDHIQMAJ64cYMfz4hWrIA)

```sh
--parser typescript
```

**Input:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
namespace F // c
{ a; }
```

**Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
namespace F { // c
  a;
}
```

**Second Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
namespace F {
  // c
  a;
}
```

### Expected output
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
enum F {
  // c
  A,
}

namespace F {
  // c
  a;
}
```

### Why?

The first format prints the comment after `{`, and the second format moves it to its own line in the body. A class and an interface with the same comment (`class F // c` + `{ a = 1 }`) print it on its own line in the body on the first format, and that output is stable.

Related, but a different case: #12593 (comment in an empty enum body).

Also reproduces on `main` (88d8e96).

**Prettier 3.9.9**
[Playground link](https://prettier.io/playground/#N4Igxg9gdgLgprEAuEBDARgZxgJ1WGAAjgA8AHCHIsAG1U00IEFDgBfAHShABoQIyMAJbRMyUGVQ5McHMhAwAnmTiYwOIYJBs2QA)

```sh
--parser typescript
```

**Input:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
abstract export class A {}
```

**Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
abstract class A {}
```

**Expected output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
abstract export class A {}
```

**Why?**

The class is no longer exported. TypeScript reports TS1029 (`'export' modifier must precede 'abstract' modifier`) for the input, but Prettier formats it and silently drops the modifier. It should either keep `export` or throw, as it does for other misplaced modifiers.

Also reproduces on `main` (88d8e96).

The class is no longer exported. TypeScript reports TS1029 (`'export' modifier must precede 'abstract' modifier`) for the input, but Prettier formats it and silently drops the modifier. It should either keep `export` or throw, as it does for other misplaced modifiers.

Also reproduces on `main` (88d8e96).

### Example 1
[Playground link](https://prettier.io/playground/#N4Igxg9gdgLgprEAucAbAhgZ0wAgMI7AA6UOOAHjgLw7ollEgCWUjAFAJSEC+JvUIADQgIABxhNomZKFHoATpjjzkIGAE9RcTGHlNxQkEoC2TZADN0qJd25A)

```sh
--parser typescript
--no-semi
```

**Input:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
class C {
  x = a
  "in"() {}
}
```

**Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
class C {
  x = a
  in() {}
}
```

**Second format** (of the output above) **fails:**
```
Expression expected. (3:6)
```

### Example 2

```sh
--parser typescript
--no-semi
```

**Input:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
interface I {
  "get"
  a: string
}
```

**Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
interface I {
  get
  a: string
}
```

**Second format** (of the output above) **fails:**
```
'(' expected. (3:4)
```

### Expected output
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
class C {
  x = a;
  in() {}
}

interface I {
  get;
  a: string
}
```

### Why?

Written unquoted in the input (`x = a;` + `in() {}`, `get;` + `a: string`), Prettier keeps the `;`. The quoted key is unquoted after that check, so the output reads as `x = a in ()…` and as a `get a` accessor, and neither parses.

Related: #1875 (the same for keys written unquoted, fixed), #19618.

Also reproduces on `main` (88d8e96).

Related: #11777 (a multi-line comment after a type).

Also reproduces on `main` (88d8e96).

[Playground link](https://prettier.io/playground/#N4Igxg9gdgLgprEAuEAzAFAOmwHSgAnwHoAqfMfEovQgQwEoBuPEAGhAgAcYBLaAZ2ShOtAE784o5CBgBPTnH5hRPbiAC+6oA)

```sh
--parser typescript
```

**Input:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
f(...
  /* c */
  a);
```

**Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
f(
  .../* c */
  a,
);
```

**Second Output:**
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
f(.../* c */ a);
```

### Expected output
<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```tsx
let a: /* c */ T;

f(.../* c */ a);
```

### Why?

The first format prints `T` on the next line without indentation, and breaks the call after `.../* c */`. The second format joins the lines.

Related: #11777 (a multi-line comment after a type).

Also reproduces on `main` (88d8e96).

**Prettier main (9d6c05b)**, not in 3.9.10

i couldn't use the playground for this since its on 3.9.10 and the bug is only on main. i ran it from a main checkout with `prettier.format(input, { parser: "yaml" })`.

```sh
# Options (if any):
--parser yaml
```

**Input:**

```yaml
a:
  b: |
    x 
  c: 1
```

(there's a trailing space after `x`)

**Output:**

```yaml
a:
  b: |
    x 
c: 1
```

**Expected output:**

```yaml
a:
  b: |
    x 
  c: 1
```

**Why?**

`c: 1` gets moved out of `a` to the root, so the formatted file means something different. in a list it can even break the file, e.g. this github actions style input:

```yaml
steps:
  - run: |
      echo hi 
    name: x
  - name: second
```

comes out as

```yaml
steps:
  - run: |
      echo hi 
name: x
  - name: second
```

which doesn't parse anymore ("A block sequence may not be used as an implicit map key").

3.9.9 keeps the structure (it just strips the trailing space, which is what #19764 fixed). so i think this came in with #19764. looking at `src/language-yaml/print/block.js`, the last-line branch now emits a `literalline` when `hasTrailingContentWhitespace(node)` is true even if the block scalar isn't the last thing in its parent. that resets the indent for whatever gets printed next. probably it should only do that when the block scalar is the last node, or restore the indentation after it.

happy to send a PR with a test for the mapping and sequence cases if that helps.

i couldn't use the playground for this since its on 3.9.10 and the bug is only on main. i ran it from a main checkout with `prettier.format(input, { parser: "yaml" })`.

```sh
# Options (if any):
--parser yaml
```

**Input:**

```yaml
a:
  b: |
    x 
  c: 1
```

(there's a trailing space after `x`)

**Output:**

```yaml
a:
  b: |
    x 
c: 1
```

**Expected output:**

```yaml
a:
  b: |
    x 
  c: 1
```

**Why?**

`c: 1` gets moved out of `a` to the root, so the formatted file means something different. in a list it can even break the file, e.g. this github actions style input:

```yaml
steps:
  - run: |
      echo hi 
    name: x
  - name: second
```

comes out as

```yaml
steps:
  - run: |
      echo hi 
name: x
  - name: second
```

which doesn't parse anymore ("A block sequence may not be used as an implicit map key").

3.9.9 keeps the structure (it just strips the trailing space, which is what #19764 fixed). so i think this came in with #19764. looking at `src/language-yaml/print/block.js`, the last-line branch now emits a `literalline` when `hasTrailingContentWhitespace(node)` is true even if the block scalar isn't the last thing in its parent. that resets the indent for whatever gets printed next. probably it should only do that when the block scalar is the last node, or restore the indentation after it.

happy to send a PR with a test for the mapping and sequence cases if that helps.

body_text:
This library adds a dependency on the unmaintained json-iterator library in the `api/prometheus/v1` package

It looks like it does this for two reasons:
1. To add more efficient unmarshalers for specific types from `github.com/prometheus/common/model`
2. To do more efficient internal unmarshaling for types declared in `api/prometheus/v1`

In addition to being unmaintained, the json-iterator library also achieves some of its efficiency at the cost of correctness and proper use of Go APIs (there is extensive use of unsafe, as well as linking to internal go functions that have caused breakages when bumping Go minor versions). This library is the [last one in the Kubernetes tree](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b2ec8b6fefac451a2dedafc4dd71f2f16c7a6abe/hack/unwanted-dependencies.json#L159-L161) that pulls in json-iterator as a dependency, and we're trying to eliminate it from our dependency tree if we can.

With Go 1.27, json/v2 provides the ability to implement custom streaming json encode/decode methods that are very close to the custom json-iterator implementations in performance. In my experiments, they were ~equivalent to the json-iterator allocs and slightly better in bytes used (in addition to being more correct and matching the default json serializations for `github.com/prometheus/common/model`).

I propose we:
1. Benchmark json and json/v2 in `api/prometheus/v1/api_bench_test.go`
2. Implement UnmarshalJSONFrom methods on `github.com/prometheus/common/model` types in go1.27-build-tagged files with equivalence tests to ensure identical behavior to the UnmarshalJSON methods
3. Once benchmarks demonstrate that we have good enough performance using stdlib with streaming json implementations, limit the json-iterator implementations to Go 1.26 and below
4. Once Go 1.26 goes out of support in February 2027, drop the Go 1.26-tagged json-iterator implementations at that point and collapse onto stdlib.

PRs:
- https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/pull/2107
- https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/pull/2109
- https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/pull/2110
- https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/pull/2111

- https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/pull/2138
- https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/pull/2128
- https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/pull/2141

{"repository": "prometheus/client_golang", "task_candidate_id": 19302, "repository_id": 211, "issue_number": 2105, "github_issue_id": 5356135517, "html_url": "https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/issues/2105", "created_at": "2026-09-05T06:25:50+00:00", "author_association": "CONTRIBUTOR", "title": "Move from unmaintained json-iterator custom encoders to json/v2 encoding", "body_text": "This library adds a dependency on the unmaintained json-iterator library in the `api/prometheus/v1` package

It looks like it does this for two reasons:
1. To add more efficient unmarshalers for specific types from `github.com/prometheus/common/model`
2. To do more efficient internal unmarshaling for types declared in `api/prometheus/v1`

In addition to being unmaintained, the json-iterator library also achieves some of its efficiency at the cost of correctness and proper use of Go APIs (there is extensive use of unsafe, as well as linking to internal go functions that have caused breakages when bumping Go minor versions). This library is the [last one in the Kubernetes tree](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b2ec8b6fefac451a2dedafc4dd71f2f16c7a6abe/hack/unwanted-dependencies.json#L159-L161) that pulls in json-iterator as a dependency, and we're trying to eliminate it from our dependency tree if we can.

With Go 1.27, json/v2 provides the ability to implement custom streaming json encode/decode methods that are very close to the custom json-iterator implementations in performance. In my experiments, they were ~equivalent to the json-iterator allocs and slightly better in bytes used (in addition to being more correct and matching the default json serializations for `github.com/prometheus/common/model`).

I propose we:
1. Benchmark json and json/v2 in `api/prometheus/v1/api_bench_test.go`
2. Implement UnmarshalJSONFrom methods on `github.com/prometheus/common/model` types in go1.27-build-tagged files with equivalence tests to ensure identical behavior to the UnmarshalJSON methods
3. Once benchmarks demonstrate that we have good enough performance using stdlib with streaming json implementations, limit the json-iterator implementations to Go 1.26 and below
4. Once Go 1.26 goes out of support in February 2027, drop the Go 1.26-tagged json-iterator implementations at that point and collapse onto stdlib.

body_text: `sync.Pool` has a somewhat surprising behavior that it has processor-local copies (https://victoriametrics.com/blog/go-sync-pool/). So on large machines (mine has GOMAXPROCS=32 default), we can end up with 32 copies of items stored in sync.Pool - even without concurrent usage. Prometheus uses a pool for gzip: https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/blob/9bf26f79511fed7c5143fb78443f5590ec6836cd/prometheus/promhttp/http.go#L660. With 32 copies of the gzip writer, we end up with ~10mb heap usage. Which isn't _crazy_ but is a pretty substantial amount for an otherwise very small application doing very little allocations/GC, and serving even a tiny number of metrics. The reason `sync.Pool` does this is to improve throughput by avoiding synchronization. However, in a scraping setup I would think that its very uncommon to have much concurrency (_maybe_ you have a couple of scrapers, but I'd imagine the median is 1 scraper) Below shows my application's memory usage after disabling gzip due to this: So at least in my specific case, it seems like it might be more optimal to use a `sync.Pool`-like structure that doesn't have this per-processor copying mechanism.

body_text:
Currently we call `WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)` [before attempting to copy the response body from the source](https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/blob/de866d63fa67a78f723397d33624b89a439dbe73/prometheus/promhttp/delegator.go#L111):

```golang
	if !d.wroteHeader {
		d.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
	}
	n, err := d.ResponseWriter.(io.ReaderFrom).ReadFrom(re)
	d.written += n
	return n, err
```

In contrast, `net/http` sets 200 only after copying at least one byte, allowing for an error response to be emitted to the http client in case zero bytes were copied.

That is:
* Without promhttp, `net/http`'s own `ReadFrom()` sets 200 as part of writing the first byte of the copy (not before that):
https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.3/src/net/http/server.go#L1643-L1645
* With promhttp, 200 is always locked in; a later `http.Error(w, ..., 502)` does not _actually_ change the response status code anymore; the client gets the response with status code 200; and the instrumentation records it as `code="502"`.  


### Repro

Built with Opus 5.5; with client_golang v1.24.1, go1.26.3 and go1.27.1:

  ```go
  package main
   
  import (
        "errors"
        "fmt"
        "io"
        "net/http"
        "net/http/httptest"
        "testing/iotest"
   
        "github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus"
        "github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus/promhttp"
        "github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus/testutil"
  )
   
  func main() {
        h := http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                if _, err := io.Copy(w, iotest.ErrReader(errors.New("upstream failed"))); err != nil {
                        http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusBadGateway)
                }
        })
        c := prometheus.NewCounterVec(prometheus.CounterOpts{Name: "requests_total"}, []string{"code"})
        for _, h := range []http.Handler{h, promhttp.InstrumentHandlerCounter(c, h)} {
                resp, err := http.Get(httptest.NewServer(h).URL)
                if err != nil {
                        panic(err)
                }
                fmt.Println(resp.StatusCode)
        }
        fmt.Println(`requests_total{code="502"}`, testutil.ToFloat64(c.WithLabelValues("502")))
  }
  ```

  Output:

  ```
  502
  2026/10/06 14:09:31 http: superfluous response.WriteHeader call from
  github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus/promhttp.(*responseWriterDelegator).WriteHeader (delegator.go:65)
  200
  requests_total{code="502"} 1
  ```

### Patch?

There are multiple ways to address this, if we wanted to. We can check `n` after the copy, but `InstrumentHandlerTimeToWriteHeader` would then measure the whole copy duration. Can use an approach like https://github.com/golang/go/commit/831f9376d8d730b16fb33dfd775618dffe13ce7a instead.

Well. Maybe I am missing something here, would appreciate feedback before I even think about solutioning.

### Description

During performance and allocation analysis of `Registry.Gather()` with `BenchmarkGatherMetricVec`, memory profiling (`go tool pprof -alloc_objects`) revealed three hot-path sources of heap allocations during metric gathering and consistency checks:

1. **Per-metric `xxhash.Digest` allocation**: In `checkMetricConsistency`, every collected metric instantiates a new digest via `h := xxhash.New()`. For a registry with 5,000 metrics, this creates 5,000 heap allocations per scrape.
2. **Interface boxing on label sortedness check**: `checkMetricConsistency` calls `sort.IsSorted(internal.LabelPairSorter(dtoMetric.Label))`. Converting the slice `LabelPairSorter` to the `sort.Interface` causes an interface boxing allocation on the heap for every metric.
3. **Unconditional `sort.Sort` on MetricFamily metrics**: In `internal.NormalizeMetricFamilies()`, `sort.Sort(MetricSorter(mf.Metric))` is called on every metric family even when `len(mf.Metric) <= 1`.

### Impact

On large registries with thousands of metrics, these three items contribute to millions of unnecessary short-lived heap allocations, increasing GC frequency and CPU overhead on each scrape.

### Proposed Solution

1. Use a `sync.Pool` to pool and reuse `*xxhash.Digest` in `Gather()` and `Gatherers.Gather()`, resetting the digest for each metric instead of allocating a new one.
2. Introduce `internal.IsLabelPairsSorted` to verify label sorting in $O(N)$ with zero allocations and no interface boxing.
3. Skip `sort.Sort` in `internal.NormalizeMetricFamilies` when `len(mf.Metric) <= 1`.

I have a patch with tests and `benchstat` results ready to submit.

body_text:
### Proposal

I was reading through the stale series compaction code and I think there's a gap in what it reports.

Right now there are six metrics for stale and selected series compaction:

- `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compactions_triggered_total`
- `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compactions_failed_total`
- `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compaction_duration_seconds`
- and the same three for selected series compaction

All of them tell you the compaction ran. None of them tell you whether it actually freed anything.

That matters because eviction is deliberately conservative. `truncateStaleSeries` skips a series if it picked up out of order data, got a new sample, or its fingerprint changed while the block was being written. So a run can go through 50k candidates and evict zero of them, and from the outside it looks identical to a run that evicted all of them. Triggered counter goes up, failed counter stays flat, duration gets recorded, done.

The log line doesn't really help either:

```go
db.logger.Info("Ending stale series compaction", "num_series", len(staleSeriesRefs.sortedByRef), "duration", elapsed)
```

`num_series` there is the candidate count, not the number that got evicted. So a run that freed nothing still logs `num_series=50000`, which reads like it worked.

The slightly odd part is the number already exists. `truncateSeries` returns `len(deleted)` and both callers throw it away:

```go
func (h *Head) truncateStaleSeries(...) error {
	_, err := h.truncateSeries(seriesRefs, maxt, func(s *memSeries) bool {
```

Same thing in `truncateSelectedSeries`.

I checked whether `prometheus_tsdb_head_series_removed_total` covers it and it doesn't. That one gets incremented from four different places (WAL replay, normal head gc, this path, and `deleteSeriesByID`), so you can't pull stale compaction out of it.

Why I think it's worth adding: `stale_series_compaction_threshold` is opt in and still experimental, so the people running it are exactly the people who need to know if it's helping. In #18379 someone turned it on, hit problems, and was debugging off a memory graph because there wasn't anything better to look at.

I hit a smaller version of this myself while writing a test against this code. I spent a while assuming eviction was happening when it actually wasn't, and only worked it out by reading `head.metrics.seriesRemoved` directly. An operator can't do that.

What I'd suggest:

- counters for candidates and evicted per compaction type, so something like `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compaction_series_candidates_total` and `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compaction_series_evicted_total`, plus the selected series versions
- add `num_evicted` to both log lines, and leave `num_series` alone so nothing parsing logs breaks

Both numbers are useful since evicted over candidates is the thing you'd actually alert on, and you can't work one out from the other with what's there today. If four new metrics feels like too many, just the evicted ones would still fix the main problem.

The change itself is small. The count already gets computed, it just needs returning instead of dropping, and the callers can capture it in the closure they already pass so `headSeriesEvictor` doesn't need to change.

I was reading through the stale series compaction code and I think there's a gap in what it reports.

Right now there are six metrics for stale and selected series compaction:

- `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compactions_triggered_total`
- `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compactions_failed_total`
- `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compaction_duration_seconds`
- and the same three for selected series compaction

All of them tell you the compaction ran. None of them tell you whether it actually freed anything.

That matters because eviction is deliberately conservative. `truncateStaleSeries` skips a series if it picked up out of order data, got a new sample, or its fingerprint changed while the block was being written. So a run can go through 50k candidates and evict zero of them, and from the outside it looks identical to a run that evicted all of them. Triggered counter goes up, failed counter stays flat, duration gets recorded, done.

The log line doesn't really help either:

```go
db.logger.Info("Ending stale series compaction", "num_series", len(staleSeriesRefs.sortedByRef), "duration", elapsed)
```

`num_series` there is the candidate count, not the number that got evicted. So a run that freed nothing still logs `num_series=50000`, which reads like it worked.

The slightly odd part is the number already exists. `truncateSeries` returns `len(deleted)` and both callers throw it away:

```go
func (h *Head) truncateStaleSeries(...) error {
	_, err := h.truncateSeries(seriesRefs, maxt, func(s *memSeries) bool {
```

Same thing in `truncateSelectedSeries`.

I checked whether `prometheus_tsdb_head_series_removed_total` covers it and it doesn't. That one gets incremented from four different places (WAL replay, normal head gc, this path, and `deleteSeriesByID`), so you can't pull stale compaction out of it.

Why I think it's worth adding: `stale_series_compaction_threshold` is opt in and still experimental, so the people running it are exactly the people who need to know if it's helping. In #18379 someone turned it on, hit problems, and was debugging off a memory graph because there wasn't anything better to look at.

I hit a smaller version of this myself while writing a test against this code. I spent a while assuming eviction was happening when it actually wasn't, and only worked it out by reading `head.metrics.seriesRemoved` directly. An operator can't do that.

What I'd suggest:

- counters for candidates and evicted per compaction type, so something like `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compaction_series_candidates_total` and `prometheus_tsdb_stale_series_compaction_series_evicted_total`, plus the selected series versions
- add `num_evicted` to both log lines, and leave `num_series` alone so nothing parsing logs breaks

Both numbers are useful since evicted over candidates is the thing you'd actually alert on, and you can't work one out from the other with what's there today. If four new metrics feels like too many, just the evicted ones would still fix the main problem.

The change itself is small. The count already gets computed, it just needs returning instead of dropping, and the callers can capture it in the closure they already pass so `headSeriesEvictor` doesn't need to change.

### What did you do?

### Context

I am moving scrape jobs to service discovery (`http_sd_configs`) where the SD endpoint provides the scrape interval per target via the `__scrape_interval__` label, so intervals are managed centrally instead of in each job. Some exporters compute metrics dynamically at scrape time and need several minutes to respond, so they use a long interval (5m) and a long timeout (4m).

I first reported this against vmagent (VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics#11597). While investigating, the VictoriaMetrics maintainer compared behavior with Prometheus and found that Prometheus has the same underlying issue: the scrape timeout is resolved and validated at job level, before per-target `__scrape_interval__` is known.

### Case A: explicit job-level timeout, interval provided by SD

```yaml
global:
  scrape_interval: 1m
  scrape_timeout: 1m

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: example
    scrape_timeout: 4m
    # no scrape_interval: provided per target by SD
    http_sd_configs:
      - url: http://sd.example/targets
```

SD response:

```json
[
  {
    "targets": ["target.example:9100"],
    "labels": { "__scrape_interval__": "5m" }
  }
]
```

### Case B: timeout inherited from global, job interval overridden by SD

```yaml
global:
  scrape_interval: 1m
  scrape_timeout: 1m

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: example
    scrape_interval: 40s
    http_sd_configs:
      - url: http://sd.example/targets
```

Same SD response as above (`__scrape_interval__: 5m`).

### What did you expect to see?

The timeout should be resolved and checked against the **final per-target** scrape interval, after SD labels and relabeling are applied:

- Case A: the target is accepted with `__scrape_interval__="5m"` and `__scrape_timeout__="4m"`, since 4m < 5m.
- Case B: `__scrape_interval__="5m"` and `__scrape_timeout__="1m"`. The only timeout setting is the global 1m, which is valid against the 5m per-target interval.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

- Case A: Prometheus refuses to load the configuration:
  `scrape timeout greater than scrape interval for scrape config with job name "example"`
  The job's `scrape_timeout` is compared with the global interval (1m) inherited by the job, even though every target from SD has a 5m interval.

- Case B: the target gets `__scrape_interval__="5m"` and `__scrape_timeout__="40s"`. The default timeout is capped to the job-level interval (40s) at config load time, and this capped value is then used for targets whose SD-provided interval is 5m.

### Root cause

1. `ScrapeConfig.Validate` fills in the job interval from global, then rejects an explicit timeout that exceeds it, or caps the inherited timeout to it (`min(global timeout, job interval)`):
   https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/50461b669f0be3a9f0b31a94f72cde8e98f2779f/config/config.go#L919-L934
2. `PopulateLabels` sets `__scrape_timeout__` from this job-level value as a default target label:
   https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/50461b669f0be3a9f0b31a94f72cde8e98f2779f/scrape/target.go#L620-L625
3. After relabeling, the per-target interval and timeout are checked against each other, but the timeout is not re-derived from the final interval:
   https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/50461b669f0be3a9f0b31a94f72cde8e98f2779f/scrape/target.go#L666-L686

### Possible approach

Keep the per-target validation in `PopulateLabels` (step 3) as the source of truth, and resolve the default timeout per target from the final `__scrape_interval__` instead of at config load. The load-time check could remain for jobs where the interval cannot be overridden, or be turned into a warning.

Workaround: set `__scrape_timeout__` explicitly in the SD response or via `relabel_configs`.

Follow-up tracking issue to address the remaining open review comments from https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/18606, just to make sure it doesn't get lost.

### Bug Fixes & Parser Options

#### 1. Unescape exemplar label names with `unreplace`
- [ ] Unescape exemplar label names in `parseSingleExemplar` ([discussion](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/18606#discussion_r3812976624))

https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/ffe0b67b8156d0fa815055a80adbc757b68c63e3/model/textparse/openmetrics2parse.go#L602-L611

From @dashpole:
> ```suggestion
> 		p.builder.Add(unreplace(string(p.l.b[a:b])), unreplace(string(p.l.b[c:d])))
> ```
> Label names can contain escape sequences in OM2, so we should unescape the name with `unreplace` here like in `Labels()`.
