## Context

Part of https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16944

The four metadata metrics in [`queue_manager.go`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L134) were designed in #6815 for the **PRW1 `metadata_config.send` side channel**, where metadata is:

* sent in **separate requests** containing *only* `MetricMetadata` entries,
* **per metric family** (not per series),
* emitted **once per `send_interval`** (default 1m).

```
prometheus_remote_storage_metadata_total
prometheus_remote_storage_metadata_failed_total
prometheus_remote_storage_metadata_retried_total
prometheus_remote_storage_metadata_bytes_total
```

In **PRW2** metadata is a field of every `writev2.TimeSeries`, always encoded, attached per series, in the *same* request as samples. The old model does not map onto the new one, and today's code reflects that confusion.

This issue is to decide what these metrics should mean (or whether they should exist) for PRW2 **before we call PRW2 stable** — metric names and semantics are user-facing API, so changing them after GA is a breaking change.

<details>
<summary>
Problems observed in current `main`
</summary>

### 1. Three of the four metrics are permanently `0` under PRW2

| Metric | v1 | v2 | 
| --- | --- | --- | 
| `metadata_total` | ✅ [L638](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L638) | ✅ [L2303](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L2303) (`recordBatchAttempt`) | 
| `metadata_failed_total` | ✅ [L588](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L588) | ❌ never — `updateMetrics` doesn't even take `metadataCount` | 
| `metadata_retried_total` | ✅ [L632](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L632) | ❌ never — `recordRetry` omits metadata | 
| `metadata_bytes_total` | ✅ [L639](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L639) | ❌ never | 

A flat-zero counter is worse than an absent one: it reads as "metadata is perfectly healthy".

Note `metadata_failed_total` is arguably *not computable* in PRW2: the [`Written-*` response headers](https://prometheus.io/docs/specs/prw/remote_write_spec_2_0/#required-written-response-headers) only report samples, histograms and exemplars, so there is no receiver-reported metadata stat to diff against, the way [`updateMetrics`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L1717) does for the other types.

### 2. `metadata_total` silently changes meaning by ~3 orders of magnitude

* v1 rate ≈ `metric_families / send_interval` (e.g. ~500/60s).
* v2 rate ≈ **samples rate**, because every batched series that carries metadata is counted, on every send attempt.

Same metric name, same queue, wildly different magnitude. Any dashboard/alert/report comparing `metadata_total` to `samples_total`, or trending it across a v1 → v2 migration, breaks silently.

### 3. `bytes_total` HELP text is wrong under PRW2

> "The total number of bytes of **data (not metadata)** sent by the queue after compression."

Under PRW2, help/unit strings live in the symbols table of the very same request, so metadata bytes *are* counted in `bytes_total` — while `metadata_bytes_total` stays 0.

### 4. The counting rule in `populateV2TimeSeries` is incoherent

In [`populateV2TimeSeries`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L1975):

* `type-and-unit-labels` branch: type **and** unit are always written into the request, but `nPendingMetadata++` only happens **if help exists** → undercount.
* `default` branch: a `Metadata{Type: UNKNOWN}` message *is* still encoded and sent → counted as nothing.
* So the counter is neither "series carrying metadata" nor "series with complete metadata".

Also, `nUnexpectedMetadata` (a `tMetadata` record reaching the v2 path, which should be impossible) is only [logged as a warning](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L1610) — no counter, so it is invisible in monitoring.

### 5. Out-of-the-box PRW2 reports zero metadata while logging the opposite

With defaults (no `metadata-wal-records`, no `type-and-unit-labels`), `seriesMetadata` is never populated, so `metadata_total == 0` forever — yet we log:

> `usage of 'metadata_config.send' is redundant when using remote write v2 (or higher) as metadata will always be gathered from the WAL and included for every series within each write request`

which is only true with the opt-in `metadata-wal-records` feature flag. A user migrating v1 → v2 sees metadata_total go to zero, reads the log saying it's fine, and has no signal telling them which is true.

### 6. The question users actually need answered is *coverage*, and we don't expose it

For PRW2 the interesting questions are:

1. Is metadata flowing at all, and where does it come from (WAL records / type-and-unit labels / nothing)?
2. What fraction of sent series carry type / unit / help?

The receiver side already has [`prometheus_api_remote_write_without_metadata_appended_samples_total`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/storage/remote/write_handler.go#L70). There is no sender-side counterpart.

</details>

### TL;DR Prometheus lets operators rewrite **labels** freely (`metric_relabel_configs`, `write_relabel_configs`), but gives them **no supported way to rewrite metadata** — `TYPE`, `UNIT`, `HELP`. Metadata is whatever the target or sender said it was, forever. That was tolerable while metadata was decorative. We are slowly in the world where it no longer is: with [PROM-39](https://github.com/prometheus/proposals/blob/main/proposals/2024-09-25_metadata-labels.md) / `--enable-feature=type-and-unit-labels`, type and unit are part of series identity, selectable in PromQL, [drive `rate()` counter-ness annotations](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/promql/engine.go#L2445-L2462), and are necessary for downstream systems e.g. OpenTelemetry and Google. **Wrong metadata could be now assumed as actively harmful, and users cannot fix it in Prometheus.** This issue is primarily a **collection of use cases** to see if we have some consensus to add such mechanism to Prometheus (or other use cases I am missing). Proper proposal should be done, but I wanted to gather feedback first. ## Use cases ### 1. Specifying a missing or wrong type, unit or help ##### Example: The exporter miss `# TYPE` (or says `untyped`) A large share of exposition in the wild is untyped: textfile collector output, `statsd_exporter`, JMX exporter, home-grown `/metrics` handlers, legacy vendor agents. ``` # HELP myapp_requests_total Total requests. myapp_requests_total{route="/api"} 4213 ``` The operator knows well this is a counter. They cannot patch the exporter (third party, vendored, or 200 teams own it). With type-aware PromQL UX they now get warned — or silently degraded — forever on metrics they don't own. > **Wants:** "for this job, anything matching `myapp_.*_total` is a counter." ##### Example: No `# UNIT` (impossible in Prometheus text format anyway) The name encodes milliseconds. The operator wants `__unit__="milliseconds"` so unit-aware UI formatting and future unit-aware functions work. The inverse also happens: an exporter declares a misleading unit that the operator wants to strip. ``` # TYPE http_request_latency_ms gauge http_request_latency_ms 12.5 ``` > **Wants:** derive `__unit__` from a name suffix, or set/clear it outright. ##### Example: RW/OTLP parity metadata fixed on RW or OTLP receive OTel users have the Collector `transform` processor: ```yaml transform: metric_statements: - set(metric.unit, "s") where metric.name == "foo" - set(metric.description, "") ``` Pushing OTLP **directly** to Prometheus loses this entirely: `OTLPConfig` exposes nine fixed knobs and no transform hook. Users end up deploying a whole Collector purely to fix a unit string. > **Wants:** the same metadata fixes available on the OTLP and RW receive path. ### 2. Do certain relabelling based on type, unit ##### Example: Rename all __type__==counter without _total suffix to have _total suffix. > **Wants:** perform relabel action based on metadata Today this **silently drops the metadata** — the family match is done against the post-relabel name. If we let users rename, we should let them restate the metadata that goes with the new name. > **Wants:** rename and metadata stay consistent, or can be re-declared in the same block. ### 3. Dropping huge `HELP` strings Real-world exporters ship multi-kilobyte `HELP` text: whole paragraphs, embedded JSON, even stack traces. That costs head memory, WAL bytes, and Remote Write 2.0 bandwidth — repeated per series. There is no knob for this today short of all-or-nothing `metadata_config.send: false` (RW1 only), which also throws away type and unit. > **Wants:** "drop HELP for this job" / "truncate HELP to N bytes" / "drop HELP only for these metrics."

body_text:
### What did you do?

I rendered the complete `PrometheusRemoteStorageFailures` rule from [the current mixin](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d/documentation/prometheus-mixin/alerts.libsonnet#L186-L207) at `c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d` and ran synthetic 1m counter traces through `promtool 3.15.0 test rules` (fixtures below). The source [increments `samples_total` on each Store attempt](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L1797-L1843); [the queue test confirms this](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d/storage/remote/queue_manager_test.go#L191-L193).

### What did you expect to see?

When all 100 sent samples fail terminally, report 100% failed, not 50%. For a steady completed-retry trace with 400 attempts, 300 retries and 2 terminal failures per minute (100 distinct first sends), the 2% terminal-failure fraction should remain above the 1% threshold for 15m.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

`promtool test rules observed.test.yml` passes: the annotation says 50.0% in the all-failed case, while the retry trace emits no alert at 30m. `promtool test rules intent.test.yml` fails exactly those two expectations (100.0% versus 50.0%; expected alert versus none). This arises with the legacy `samples_total` fallback: the rule divides `failed` by `failed + samples_total`, counting terminal failures twice and treating retry attempts as more samples. It still needs to support both legacy metric aliases.

A simple `samples_total - samples_retried_total` denominator is not a proven fix: canceled backoff can count a retry with no subsequent attempt; hard shutdown can count failures with no send; accepted subsets may have incomplete/overlapping v1 response stats; and attempts/retries can land on opposite sides of a 5m rate window. `promtool test rules edge.test.yml` passes expression controls for cancellation/window arithmetic. Could we agree on the intended alert population (attempts, terminal outcomes, or distinct samples) before changing the rule or instrumentation? I found this while studying alert rules across projects; results are published only in aggregate.

### Environment

Synthetic promtool fixture only; macOS darwin/arm64, `promtool 3.15.0`. No live remote-write incident or deployment asserted. Prometheus source pin: `c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d`.


AI tools assisted with the analysis and synthetic tests.

Save each block under the indicated filename and run `promtool test rules observed.test.yml intent.test.yml edge.test.yml`. The two intent failures are expected on the current rule.

# Rendered from documentation/prometheus-mixin/config.libsonnet + alerts.libsonnet
# at c45b13bbdd96b47a5441000fb454dce42894349d; only this alert retained.
"groups":
- "name": "prometheus"
  "rules":
  - "alert": "PrometheusRemoteStorageFailures"
    "annotations":
      "description": "Prometheus {{$labels.instance}} failed to send {{ printf \"%.1f\" $value }}% of the samples to {{ $labels.remote_name}}:{{ $labels.url }}"
      "summary": "Prometheus fails to send samples to remote storage."
    "expr": |
      (
        (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_failed_samples_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]))
      /
        (
          (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_failed_samples_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]))
        +
          (rate(prometheus_remote_storage_succeeded_samples_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]) or rate(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_total{job="prometheus"}[5m]))
        )
      )
      * 100
      > 1
    "for": "15m"
    "labels":
      "severity": "critical"

```

# Arithmetic controls for the subtract-retries PROTOTYPE, not a proposed fix.
# Source allows onRetry after ctx.Done during backoff, before a subsequent Store;
# metric increments can also straddle the 5m window boundary.
rule_files:
  - rule.yml
evaluation_interval: 1m
tests:
  - name: cancellation_after_first_attempt_retry_counter_without_second_attempt
    interval: 1m
    input_series:
      - series: 'prometheus_remote_storage_samples_total{job="prometheus"}'
        values: '0 100 100 100 100 100 100 100 100 100'
      - series: 'prometheus_remote_storage_samples_retried_total{job="prometheus"}'
        values: '0 0 100 100 100 100 100 100 100 100'
      - series: 'prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total{job="prometheus"}'
        values: '0 0 0 100 100 100 100 100 100 100'
    promql_expr_test:
      - expr: 'increase(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_total[5m]) - increase(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_retried_total[5m])'
        eval_time: 5m
        exp_samples:
          - labels: '{job="prometheus"}'
            value: -100
      - expr: '100 * increase(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total[5m]) / (increase(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_total[5m]) - increase(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_retried_total[5m]))'
        eval_time: 5m
        exp_samples:
          - labels: '{job="prometheus"}'
            value: -100
  - name: first_attempt_and_retry_cross_five_minute_boundary
    interval: 1m
    input_series:
      - series: 'prometheus_remote_storage_samples_total{job="prometheus"}'
        values: '0 100 100 100 100 100 200 200 200 200 200'
      - series: 'prometheus_remote_storage_samples_retried_total{job="prometheus"}'
        values: '0 0 0 0 100 100 100 100 100 100 100'
    promql_expr_test:

        exp_samples:

            value: -100
      - expr: 'increase(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_total[5m]) - increase(prometheus_remote_storage_samples_retried_total[5m])'
        eval_time: 9m
        exp_samples:

            value: 125

### What did you do?

Similar to https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/19887 but slightly different.

If you have a simple scrape job like this:

```
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: http-job
    http_sd_configs:
      - url: http://sd.example/a
```

you'll get `prometheus_sd_refresh_*` metrics like 

```
prometheus_sd_refresh_failures_total{config="http-job",mechanism="http"} 2
```

then try renaming that `job_name` and reloading Prometheus, checking /metrics again.

### What did you expect to see?

I expected to see the `config` update with the new job name.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Instead, the old metric sticks around with `config` not updating with the new job name. This is not fixed by https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19878, that fix is limited to this other similar issue. sorry if it is all confusing :( https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19878

body_text:
Related to [prometheus#11969](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/11969), [prometheus#17864](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/17864), [prometheus#19555](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19555), and [prometheus#19563](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19563).

### Motivation

Recording rules currently write samples to storage without metric metadata (`type`, `help`, `unit`). Because of this, recorded series are missing from `/api/v1/metadata`, carry empty metadata in WAL records and Remote Write 2.0, and lack `__type__` / `__unit__` when `type-and-unit-labels` is enabled.

Storing metadata for recording rules solves several problems:

- Humans and AI agents rely on `/api/v1/metadata` (and UIs like Grafana's metrics explorer) to discover metrics, understand what a pre-computed rule represents, and autocomplete PromQL queries.
- Strongly typed backends receiving data via Remote Write 2.0 or OTLP (such as Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus) require a valid metric type for every series and have to fall back or reject untyped recorded metrics.
- Type-aware query engines, linters, and type-based aggregations need to know whether a recorded series is a float gauge, a counter, or a native histogram.

### Sketch of solution

Working on a formal proposal, but the rough idea is as follow:

Rule manager migrated to `AppenderV2` already. Through [`headAppenderV2.Append`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/6e69e843b38d22ded60a13e0163f6326136f59fa/tsdb/head_append_v2.go#L226), this populates WAL metadata records, Remote Write 2.0 metadata, `type-and-unit-labels`, and the native TSDB metadata store ([prometheus#19563](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19563)).

#### Expand manual config in `rulefmt`

Extend recording rule definitions in [`model/rulefmt`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/model/rulefmt/rulefmt.go#L186-L196) so users can optionally specify `help`, `type`, and `unit` (as explored in [prometheus#17864](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/17864) and [prometheus#19555](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19555)):

```yaml
groups:
  - name: example
    rules:
      - record: job:http_requests:rate5m
        expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
        help: "Per-job HTTP request rate over 5 minutes."
        type: gauge
        unit: requests_per_second
```

Any explicitly configured field overrides the automatically deduced value (see below), and `promtool check rules` validates that `type` is a known OpenMetrics / Prometheus metric type.

#### Automatic metadata deduction (feature flag / config option)

Add a feature flag and configuration setting to automatically populate type for recording rules without requiring users to annotate every existing rule file.

- For float samples (`s.H == nil`), defaulting to `gauge` could be a sufficient heuristic. Almost all float recording rules (`rate()`, `increase()`, `histogram_quantile()`, `avg()`, arithmetic) produce values that can go up and down. Even aggregating counters without `rate()`, like `sum by (job) (http_requests_total)`, is not a monotonic counter in practice because series churn when targets restart or disappear causes the sum to decrease without a counter reset.
- For native histogram samples (`s.H != nil`), `gaugehistogram` is likely a sufficient choice. We can inspect `s.H.CounterResetHint` ([`model/histogram/histogram.go#L26-L33`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/model/histogram/histogram.go#L26-L33)) on the evaluated sample: PromQL functions like `rate()`, `irate()`, `increase()`, `delta()`, and histogram subtraction already set `CounterResetHint = histogram.GaugeType` ([`promql/functions.go#L441`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/promql/functions.go#L441)). If `CounterResetHint == histogram.GaugeType`, the deduced type should be `gaugehistogram`; otherwise it should be `histogram`.
- When `type-and-unit-labels` is enabled, automatic deduction can respect those labels if present on the evaluation result and fall back to the sample-based deduction above.

{"repository": "prometheus/prometheus", "task_candidate_id": 19341, "repository_id": 212, "issue_number": 20027, "github_issue_id": 5862604814, "html_url": "https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/20027", "created_at": "2026-10-15T08:15:58+00:00", "author_association": "MEMBER", "title": "rules: store and deduce metric metadata (type, help, unit) for recording rules", "body_text": "Related to [prometheus#11969](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/11969), [prometheus#17864](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/17864), [prometheus#19555](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19555), and [prometheus#19563](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19563).

### Motivation

Recording rules currently write samples to storage without metric metadata (`type`, `help`, `unit`). Because of this, recorded series are missing from `/api/v1/metadata`, carry empty metadata in WAL records and Remote Write 2.0, and lack `__type__` / `__unit__` when `type-and-unit-labels` is enabled.

Storing metadata for recording rules solves several problems:

- Humans and AI agents rely on `/api/v1/metadata` (and UIs like Grafana's metrics explorer) to discover metrics, understand what a pre-computed rule represents, and autocomplete PromQL queries.
- Strongly typed backends receiving data via Remote Write 2.0 or OTLP (such as Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus) require a valid metric type for every series and have to fall back or reject untyped recorded metrics.
- Type-aware query engines, linters, and type-based aggregations need to know whether a recorded series is a float gauge, a counter, or a native histogram.

### Sketch of solution

Working on a formal proposal, but the rough idea is as follow:

Rule manager migrated to `AppenderV2` already. Through [`headAppenderV2.Append`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/6e69e843b38d22ded60a13e0163f6326136f59fa/tsdb/head_append_v2.go#L226), this populates WAL metadata records, Remote Write 2.0 metadata, `type-and-unit-labels`, and the native TSDB metadata store ([prometheus#19563](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19563)).

#### Expand manual config in `rulefmt`

Extend recording rule definitions in [`model/rulefmt`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/model/rulefmt/rulefmt.go#L186-L196) so users can optionally specify `help`, `type`, and `unit` (as explored in [prometheus#17864](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/17864) and [prometheus#19555](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19555)):

```yaml
groups:
  - name: example
    rules:
      - record: job:http_requests:rate5m
        expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
        help: "Per-job HTTP request rate over 5 minutes."
        type: gauge
        unit: requests_per_second
```

Any explicitly configured field overrides the automatically deduced value (see below), and `promtool check rules` validates that `type` is a known OpenMetrics / Prometheus metric type.

#### Automatic metadata deduction (feature flag / config option)

Add a feature flag and configuration setting to automatically populate type for recording rules without requiring users to annotate every existing rule file.

- For float samples (`s.H == nil`), defaulting to `gauge` could be a sufficient heuristic. Almost all float recording rules (`rate()`, `increase()`, `histogram_quantile()`, `avg()`, arithmetic) produce values that can go up and down. Even aggregating counters without `rate()`, like `sum by (job) (http_requests_total)`, is not a monotonic counter in practice because series churn when targets restart or disappear causes the sum to decrease without a counter reset.
- For native histogram samples (`s.H != nil`), `gaugehistogram` is likely a sufficient choice. We can inspect `s.H.CounterResetHint` ([`model/histogram/histogram.go#L26-L33`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/model/histogram/histogram.go#L26-L33)) on the evaluated sample: PromQL functions like `rate()`, `irate()`, `increase()`, `delta()`, and histogram subtraction already set `CounterResetHint = histogram.GaugeType` ([`promql/functions.go#L441`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/10f69629039e0215d056eb4948f0bd0fd22f5c89/promql/functions.go#L441)). If `CounterResetHint == histogram.GaugeType`, the deduced type should be `gaugehistogram`; otherwise it should be `histogram`.
- When `type-and-unit-labels` is enabled, automatic deduction can respect those labels if present on the evaluation result and fall back to the sample-based deduction above.

body_text:
## What happened

`PrometheusNotificationQueueRunningFull` in `documentation/prometheus-mixin/alerts.libsonnet` can never fire on a current Prometheus. Its expression compares two series that no longer carry the same labels:

```
predict_linear(prometheus_notifications_queue_length{...}[5m], 60 * 30)
>
min_over_time(prometheus_notifications_queue_capacity{...}[5m])
```

`prometheus_notifications_queue_length` has an `alertmanager` label (one series per Alertmanager URL). `prometheus_notifications_queue_capacity` does not. A binary operator pairs series on their full label set, so the two sides never match and the result is always empty. The rule loads, reports `health="ok"` and `state="inactive"`, and stays that way even with a full queue, so nothing looks wrong.

## Evidence

Prometheus v3.15.0, one Prometheus with one Alertmanager target:

```
prometheus_notifications_queue_length{alertmanager="http://10.244.1.91:9093/api/v2/alerts", instance=..., job=...}   -> 1 series
prometheus_notifications_queue_capacity{instance=..., job=...}                                                      -> 1 series
```

The left side has an extra `alertmanager` label, so 0 pairs match. Observed on the kube-prometheus-stack 88.6.2 copy of the rule, which is generated from this mixin.

## Expected

The alert fires when the notification queue is predicted to fill within 30 minutes.

## Suggested fix

Drop the `alertmanager` label from the left side so both sides have the same labels:

```
(
  max without (alertmanager) (
    predict_linear(prometheus_notifications_queue_length{%(prometheusSelector)s}[5m], 60 * 30)
  )
>
  min_over_time(prometheus_notifications_queue_capacity{%(prometheusSelector)s}[5m])
)
```

`max` takes the fullest queue, which is the one to alert on. `ignoring(alertmanager)` alone is not enough: with more than one Alertmanager it turns the mismatch into many-to-one matching and errors. I run this corrected copy in production; the same fix was made downstream in thaum-xyz/ankhmorpork#1274.

I can send a PR if that is welcome.

body_text:
### What did you do?

I ran the TSDB head with XOR2 float chunks and `EnableSTAsZeroSample` (`created-timestamp-zero-ingestion`), but without `EnableSTStorage` (`st-storage`). XOR2 can be enabled on its own, with `storage.tsdb.chunk_encoding.floats: xor2` or `--enable-feature=xor2-encoding`. I appended 100 samples of a counter through `AppenderV2`, each with the counter's start timestamp, and one sample per commit, like a scrape. Then I restarted the head from its WAL.

### What did you expect to see?

No start timestamps stored, since `st-storage` is off. The `HeadOptions.EnableSTStorage` doc comment says it "determines whether databases (WAL/WBL, tsdb, agent) should set a Start Time value per sample".

### What did you see instead?

The start timestamps are stored in the head chunk anyway. On commit, the head passes each sample's `ST` to `memSeries.append`, which passes it to the chunk appender whether or not `storeST` is set. XOR2 stores it. The WAL follows `EnableSTStorage` and doesn't record it, so the start timestamps are gone after WAL replay:

| | Chunk bytes | Start timestamps in the chunk |
|---|---|---|
| Before restart | 439 | 0 ×1 (the zero sample), 1000000 ×100 |
| After WAL replay | 142 | 0 ×101 |

So the same data is encoded differently depending on whether it was replayed. Chunks m-mapped before a restart keep their start timestamps, and data rebuilt from the WAL doesn't. The difference carries over into compacted blocks. The chunk is this big because of the zero sample's start timestamp, which is #20067.

Should the head pass `st = 0` to the chunk appenders when `storeST` is false? That covers `append`, `appendHistogram`, `appendFloatHistogram`, and `insert` for out-of-order samples. I've only checked floats, but ST-capable histogram chunks (`histograms-st-encoding`) presumably behave the same.

This matters more once XOR2 becomes the default (#19080). Every `created-timestamp-zero-ingestion` user would then write start timestamps into chunks without enabling `st-storage`. I found this while reviewing Grafana Mimir's switch to `AppenderV2`, where the first chunk of a new series grew by about 2.7×.

Reproduction, in package `tsdb` on `main` (79cee8108):

```go
func dumpHeadChunk(t *testing.T, h *Head, lbls labels.Labels) {
	s := h.series.getByHash(lbls.Hash(), lbls)
	s.Lock()
	defer s.Unlock()
	c := s.headChunks.chunk
	sts := map[int64]int{}
	it := c.Iterator(nil)
	for it.Next() == chunkenc.ValFloat {
		sts[it.AtST()]++
	}
	t.Logf("chunk bytes=%d, start timestamps=%v", len(c.Bytes()), sts)
}

func TestSTInXOR2ChunksWithoutSTStorage(t *testing.T) {
	lbls := labels.FromStrings("__name__", "c_total")
	const st = int64(1_000_000)
	newHead := func(dir string) *Head {
		opts := DefaultHeadOptions()
		opts.ChunkDirRoot = dir
		opts.FloatChunkEncoding.Store(uint32(chunkenc.EncXOR2))
		opts.EnableSTAsZeroSample = true // EnableSTStorage stays false.
		w, err := wlog.New(nil, nil, filepath.Join(dir, "wal"), compression.None)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		h, err := NewHead(nil, nil, w, nil, opts, nil)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		require.NoError(t, h.Init(0))
		return h
	}

	dir := t.TempDir()
	h := newHead(dir)
	for i := int64(1); i <= 100; i++ {
		app := h.AppenderV2(t.Context())
		_, err := app.Append(0, lbls, st, st+i*60_000, float64(i), nil, nil, storage.AOptions{})
		require.NoError(t, err)
		require.NoError(t, app.Commit())
	}
	dumpHeadChunk(t, h, lbls) // chunk bytes=439, start timestamps=map[0:1 1000000:100]
	require.NoError(t, h.Close())

	h = newHead(dir) // Replays the WAL.
	defer h.Close()
	dumpHeadChunk(t, h, lbls) // chunk bytes=142, start timestamps=map[0:101]
}
```

### Prometheus version

`main` at 79cee8108.

I ran the TSDB head with XOR2 float chunks and `EnableSTAsZeroSample` (`created-timestamp-zero-ingestion`), but without `EnableSTStorage` (`st-storage`). XOR2 can be enabled on its own, with `storage.tsdb.chunk_encoding.floats: xor2` or `--enable-feature=xor2-encoding`. I appended 100 samples of a counter through `AppenderV2`, each with the counter's start timestamp, and one sample per commit, like a scrape. Then I restarted the head from its WAL.

### What did you expect to see?

No start timestamps stored, since `st-storage` is off. The `HeadOptions.EnableSTStorage` doc comment says it "determines whether databases (WAL/WBL, tsdb, agent) should set a Start Time value per sample".

### What did you see instead?

The start timestamps are stored in the head chunk anyway. On commit, the head passes each sample's `ST` to `memSeries.append`, which passes it to the chunk appender whether or not `storeST` is set. XOR2 stores it. The WAL follows `EnableSTStorage` and doesn't record it, so the start timestamps are gone after WAL replay:

| | Chunk bytes | Start timestamps in the chunk |
|---|---|---|
| Before restart | 439 | 0 ×1 (the zero sample), 1000000 ×100 |
| After WAL replay | 142 | 0 ×101 |

So the same data is encoded differently depending on whether it was replayed. Chunks m-mapped before a restart keep their start timestamps, and data rebuilt from the WAL doesn't. The difference carries over into compacted blocks. The chunk is this big because of the zero sample's start timestamp, which is #20067.

Should the head pass `st = 0` to the chunk appenders when `storeST` is false? That covers `append`, `appendHistogram`, `appendFloatHistogram`, and `insert` for out-of-order samples. I've only checked floats, but ST-capable histogram chunks (`histograms-st-encoding`) presumably behave the same.

This matters more once XOR2 becomes the default (#19080). Every `created-timestamp-zero-ingestion` user would then write start timestamps into chunks without enabling `st-storage`. I found this while reviewing Grafana Mimir's switch to `AppenderV2`, where the first chunk of a new series grew by about 2.7×.

Reproduction, in package `tsdb` on `main` (79cee8108):

func dumpHeadChunk(t *testing.T, h *Head, lbls labels.Labels) {
	s := h.series.getByHash(lbls.Hash(), lbls)
	s.Lock()
	defer s.Unlock()
	c := s.headChunks.chunk
	sts := map[int64]int{}
	it := c.Iterator(nil)
	for it.Next() == chunkenc.ValFloat {
		sts[it.AtST()]++
	}
	t.Logf("chunk bytes=%d, start timestamps=%v", len(c.Bytes()), sts)
}

func TestSTInXOR2ChunksWithoutSTStorage(t *testing.T) {
	lbls := labels.FromStrings("__name__", "c_total")
	const st = int64(1_000_000)
	newHead := func(dir string) *Head {
		opts := DefaultHeadOptions()
		opts.ChunkDirRoot = dir
		opts.FloatChunkEncoding.Store(uint32(chunkenc.EncXOR2))
		opts.EnableSTAsZeroSample = true // EnableSTStorage stays false.
		w, err := wlog.New(nil, nil, filepath.Join(dir, "wal"), compression.None)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		h, err := NewHead(nil, nil, w, nil, opts, nil)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		require.NoError(t, h.Init(0))
		return h
	}

	dir := t.TempDir()
	h := newHead(dir)
	for i := int64(1); i <= 100; i++ {
		app := h.AppenderV2(t.Context())
		_, err := app.Append(0, lbls, st, st+i*60_000, float64(i), nil, nil, storage.AOptions{})
		require.NoError(t, err)
		require.NoError(t, app.Commit())
	}
	dumpHeadChunk(t, h, lbls) // chunk bytes=439, start timestamps=map[0:1 1000000:100]
	require.NoError(t, h.Close())

	h = newHead(dir) // Replays the WAL.
	defer h.Close()
	dumpHeadChunk(t, h, lbls) // chunk bytes=142, start timestamps=map[0:101]
}

### What did you do?

Configured a `remote_write` entry with `protobuf_message: io.prometheus.write.v2.Request` and left `send_native_histograms` at its default (false), with `scrape_native_histograms: true` and `convert_classic_histograms_to_nhcb: true`, sending to an OpenTelemetry Collector `prometheus_remote_write` receiver. Prometheus 3.13.2 and 3.14.0.

### What did you expect to see?

`docs/configuration/configuration.md` says for `send_native_histograms`: "For the `io.prometheus.write.v2.Request` message, this option is noop (always true)." So the native histograms and the NHCB-converted classic histograms should be sent over the v2 message without setting it.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

No histograms leave Prometheus. `QueueManager.AppendHistograms` and `AppendFloatHistograms` return early when `!t.sendNativeHistograms`, and `populateV2TimeSeries` fills the histogram field only when `sendNativeHistograms` is true (`storage/remote/queue_manager.go` on `release-3.14`, same on `main`). With `send_native_histograms: true` on the same entry the histograms arrive at the receiver.

Either the documentation should say that the option is required for v2 as well, or the v2 code path should force it on as documented. The second matches the documented intent and what users of the OpenTelemetry receiver need: remote write v2 is the only message it accepts, and it drops classic histograms unless they are converted to NHCB and sent as native histograms.

### System information

Linux x86_64, Kubernetes, official quay.io/prometheus/prometheus images

### Prometheus version

```text
prometheus, version 3.13.2 and 3.14.0
```

### Prometheus configuration file

```yaml
global:
  scrape_interval: 30s
  scrape_native_histograms: true
  convert_classic_histograms_to_nhcb: true
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: sample-app
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['sample-app:8080']
remote_write:
  - url: http://otel-collector:9090/api/v1/write
    protobuf_message: io.prometheus.write.v2.Request
    # send_native_histograms not set (default false)

body_text:
The "Go tests" job runs `go test -race ./...` (through `make`) with the default 10m timeout. The `tsdb` package uses most of that time, so it sometimes fails when a runner is slow, even when no test hangs.

Recent failures (none of these PRs change `tsdb`):

- #20110, two attempts on the same commit failed, the third passed: [job 1](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/actions/runs/39510583199/job/118930302389), [job 2](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/actions/runs/39510583199/job/119097502784)
- #20099: [job](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/actions/runs/39668395700/job/119459425869)

Each failure has the same signature:

```
panic: test timed out after 10m0s
	running tests:
		TestBlockReloadInterval/one_second_interval (3s)
		TestOOOCompactionWithNormalCompaction_AppendV2/custom_buckets_float_histogram (0s)
		...
FAIL	github.com/prometheus/prometheus/tsdb	600.294s
```

The tests in the "running tests" list are different in each failure, and each of them had run for only 0 to 3 seconds. No goroutine was blocked for minutes. So this is not a hang. The package as a whole goes over the limit.

Time for `tsdb` under `-race` on green `main` runs:

| Date | Duration |
|---|---|
| 2026-07-24 | 547s |
| 2026-08-19 | 447s |
| 2026-09-14 | 529s |
| 2026-10-03 | 427s |
| 2026-10-21 (6 runs) | 407s, 458s, 484s, 545s, 557s, 596s |

A normal run uses 70% to 99% of the 600s limit, so a small slowdown makes it fail.

#18630 reported the same problem and was closed by #18632, which made `TestCancelCompactions` faster. That helped, but the margin is still very small.

Possible fixes:

1. Increase the timeout for the race run, for example `-timeout 20m`. This is a small change, but it can hide future slowdowns. If we do this, we should probably set it in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and not in `Makefile.common`, because other repos share `Makefile.common`.
2. Make the `tsdb` tests faster. For example, skip some long variants under `-race`, or let more tests run in parallel.
3. Run `tsdb` in its own CI step or job, with its own timeout.

**Describe the bug**

black can turn a lambda into a tuple. if a lambda default has a comment on its own line and the lambda sits inside parentheses that have a comment after the opening paren then black adds a comma after the lambda body

**To Reproduce**

For example, take this code:

```python
handler = (  # comment
    lambda x=(
        # comment
        1,
    ): x
)
```

And run it with these arguments:

```sh
$ black file.py
```

The resulting error is:

> cannot format file.py: INTERNAL ERROR: Black 26.10.1 on Python (CPython) 3.12.14 produced code that is not equivalent to the source

with `--fast` the file gets written like this

```python
handler = (  # comment
    lambda x=(
    # comment
    1,
    ): x,
)
```

so `handler` is now a tuple and calling it gives `TypeError: 'tuple' object is not callable`. running `black --check` on that file afterwards says it would be left unchanged so it doesn't get caught later either

**Expected behavior**

no comma after the lambda body so `handler` stays a function

**Environment**

- Black's version: 26.10.1 and main
- OS and Python version: Linux / Python 3.12.14

**Additional context**

the standalone comment splits the line inside the default's brackets and `delimiter_split` then adds a trailing comma at the end of the leftover part of the line which is outside those brackets. this shape started failing in 26.10.0 and the same code with `.__name__` after the closing paren gets the extra comma since 26.3.0 (before that black crashed on it, see #4640)

the same split with `--skip-magic-trailing-comma` also drops the needed comma in a one element subscript like `a[1,]` used as a lambda default

related to #4640 and #4296. I opened #5533 with a fix

### Summary

Black resolves a relative `cache-dir` from `[tool.black]` inside the project checkout and then calls `pickle.load()` on files under that path. Both the metadata cache and the grammar caches are affected.

A repo author can drop crafted pickle files with the expected names. If someone later runs Black on that checkout with caching enabled, the process deserializes them.

This was also shared with Tidelift security, who confirmed the tracing. It was treated as a hardening issue rather than a CVE, which matches Black not claiming untrusted-checkout safety.

### Affected code

- `src/black/files.py` — finds the project `pyproject.toml`
- `src/black/__init__.py` — accepts a relative `cache-dir` from project config and passes it into grammar init (unless `--no-cache`)
- `src/black/cache.py` — metadata cache does unrestricted `pickle.load`
- `src/blib2to3/pgen2/driver.py` + `grammar.py` — grammar cache uses a predictable filename + mtime check, then `pickle.load`

### Preconditions

- Project sets a relative `cache-dir`
- Matching cache files exist for the Black version/mode/Python runtime
- Someone runs Black on the checkout with caching enabled
- `--no-cache` is not used

Cloning alone is not enough.

### Impact

Arbitrary Python code can run as the Black process. Likelihood is limited because the victim has to actually run Black with caching on, and the attacker needs the right filenames.

`--no-cache` blocks both paths.

### Suggested remediation

- Don’t accept `cache-dir` from project config (or only accept absolute paths from a trusted source)
- Switch both caches to a non-executable format, or check that the writer is the same authority as the Black process
- Treat existing project-relative pickle caches as invalid
- Keep an explicit CLI cache dir and `--no-cache` working

Static tracing only. Default cache is still per-user when there’s no project override.

First: IMHO this is related to but not a duplicate of #5871 #7222 #7219

`requests` tries to use `chardet` when it can be imported. However, IMHO it should only use it, if `requests` was installed with the `[use-chardet-on-py3]`-extra.

As reported in #7219, `requests` shows a warning, when the version of `chardet` does not fulfill the requirements. However, package managers like `uv` won't respect the version requirement of the dependency of `requests` on `chardet`, when the extra is not installed (see https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/18179). If another project dependency depends on `chardet`, it will be installed, but the version of `chardet` might not fulfill the requirement of `requests`.

The same applies to `charset_normalizer` or any other optional dependency.

## Expected Result

`chardet` should not be used, when `requests` is not installed with `[use-chardet-on-py3]`-extra.

## Actual Result

`requests` tries to use `chardet` and generates a log message complaining about an incompatible version.

## Reproduction Steps

```bash
uv init
# I use fixed versions to make the example more reproducible:
uv add tox==4.44.0 requests==2.32.5

cat > test.py <<EOF
import logging

LOGGER = logging.getLogger()
LOGGER.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

import chardet
import requests
import tox

print("tox", tox.__version__)
print("requests", requests.__version__)
print("chardet", chardet.__version__)
EOF
uv run test.py
```

#### Output:

```
.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/requests/__init__.py:113: RequestsDependencyWarning: urllib3 (2.6.3) or chardet (6.0.0.post1)/charset_normalizer (3.4.4) doesn't match a supported version!
  warnings.warn(
tox 4.44.0
requests 2.32.5
chardet 6.0.0.post1
```

  },

}

The current documentation for the `timeout` parameter in `requests.get()` does not clearly explain that it applies to both connection and read timeouts unless specified otherwise.

This can be confusing for users who expect it to behave as a total request timeout.

## Suggested Improvement

Add clarification in the docs that:
- A single float applies to both connect and read timeouts
- A tuple can be used to specify them separately

Example:
```python
requests.get(url, timeout=(connect_timeout, read_timeout))

## Announcement

Hello Requests Community,

I am the author of the @localizethedocs organization. And I’m glad to announce that the 🎉 **requests-docs-l10n** 🎉 project is published now:

- 🚀 **Preview:** [requests-docs-l10n](https://projects.localizethedocs.org/requests-docs-l10n)
- 🌐 **Crowdin:** [requests-docs-l10n](https://localizethedocs.crowdin.com/requests-docs-l10n)
- 🐙 **GitHub:** [requests-docs-l10n](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n)

The goal of this project is to translate The Requests Documentation into multiple languages. Translations are contributed via the Crowdin platform, automatically synchronized with the GitHub repository, and can be previewed on GitHub Pages.

## How to Contribute Translations?

To contribute the translations to the project, just follow the following steps:

1. Create an account on [Crowdin Enterprise](https://localizethedocs.crowdin.com/u/signup) if you don't have one.
2. Log in and go the [requests-docs-l10n](https://localizethedocs.crowdin.com/requests-docs-l10n) project.
3. Choose the language you would like to contribute.

If translators want to translate a language that is not yet supported, they just need to open a new [issue](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/issues/new?template=language_request.yml) to request the new language. Once the requested language is added, they can begin translating.

## How to Keep Content Up-to-date?

An FAQ that is sure to come up in the Requests community is: ***How to keep translations up-to-date?***

First and foremost, in my opinion, the focus should be on how to keep the **"Translatable Content (`msgid`)**" up-to-date, rather than the **"Translations (`msgstr`)**". I will focus on the most critical part of the whole infrastructure here.

In short, the [ci-sphinx-update-pot.yml](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci-sphinx-update-pot.yml) workflow will be executed weekly to check the upstream project for any required updates to the document content, which in turn triggers the update of the `.pot` files. If an update is needed, a Pull Request (PR) is automatically created to merge into the `l10n` branch. For example:

- https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/pull/2
- https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/pull/3

Once those PRs are merged, the [ci-gettext-update-po.yml](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci-gettext-update-po.yml) workflow will be triggered to merge the updated content from the `.pot` files into the `.po` files for each language. This is essentially how it keeps the "Translatable Content" up-to-date.

Therefore, the core responsibility of the code maintainers, besides ensuring the stable operation of the scripts and workflows, is to regularly _**check whether there are any pending PRs that need to be merged**_.

## How to Reuse Translations?

If the upstream project or anyone wants to reuse the translated `.po` files prepared by the `requests-docs-l10n` project, they can clone the `.po` files from the `po/${VERSION}` branch by using the following command:

```bash
git clone --depth=1 --branch=po/${VERSION} https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n.git docs/locale
```

Those `po/${VERSION}` branches are created to facilitate reusage by the upstream project. For instance, the `zh_TW` documentation for the `latest` version can be generated using the commands below:

```bash
BRANCH=main
VERSION=latest
LANGUAGE=zh_TW
BUILDER=html

# Prepare the repository and environment
git clone --branch=${BRANCH} https://github.com/psf/requests.git requests-docs
cd requests-docs
conda create --prefix ./.conda --yes
conda activate ./.conda
conda install python=3.13 -c conda-forge -c nodefaults --yes
export PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1
pip install . -r docs/requirements.txt

# Clone the .po files to the 'locale' directory
git clone --branch=po/${VERSION} --depth=1 https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n.git docs/locale

# Build the documentation
sphinx-build \
    -b ${BUILDER} \
    -D language=${LANGUAGE} \
    -D locale_dirs=locale \
    -D gettext_compact=0 \
    -D gettext_additional_targets=index,literal-block,raw \
    docs \
    docs/_build/${LANGUAGE}

# Preview the documentation
firefox docs/_build/${LANGUAGE}/index.html
```

## Related Discussions

There were issues and PRs related to documentation translations:

- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/3033
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/624
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/5902
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/5518
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/2750
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/5679
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/3221
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/2744
- https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/6142
- https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/1330
- https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/2746
- https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/2751
- https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/6144

And the @requests community **once** actively maintained documentation translations through the "source translation" method:

- Chinese: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-cn
- Japanese: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-jp
- German: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-de
- French: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-fr
- Polish: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-pl
- Portuguese: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-pt
- Dutch: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-nl
- Bulgarian: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-bg
- Arabic: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-ar
- Danish: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-da
- Italian: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-it

However, these efforts were eventually abandoned and became unmaintainable for various reasons. Notably, issue #3033 suggested migrating documentation translations to a TMS platform. Therefore, I believe that the `requests-docs-l10n` project should be able to serve this purpose.

## Summary

While using Requests, new users may encounter SSL verification errors such as:

`requests.exceptions.SSLError`

These errors can be difficult to understand for users who are unfamiliar with HTTPS certificate verification.

## Suggested Improvement

Consider adding a small troubleshooting section to the documentation covering:

- Common causes of SSL verification failures
- Basic debugging steps
- When `verify=False` may be appropriate for testing purposes
- Security implications of disabling SSL verification

## Motivation

This would improve the experience for beginners and reduce confusion when working with HTTPS requests in Requests.

Hi,

I wanted to ask the if maintainers have plans to support the newly proposed QUERY http method in the near future, as it has been awaited for more than a decade. We plan to use the method in our APIs going forward, albeit most use will be internal. I see requests is matured and in feature freeze at this time, I also understand that we can send arbitrary methods by supplying the name in the "request" method, tho it has a caveat [regarding redirections](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc10008#name-redirection).

I started some work on a fork. However before opening a PR, I wanted to make sure if you are open to contributions in this direction, as I have seen multiple recent rejections on the subject. (I have to add, rightfully so)

body_text:
> This issue is part of a larger batch of similar-scoped issues we distribute in the context of our internal vulnerability and dependency tracking activities. The batch covers multiple projects, this is only one of them. The goal is to rise awareness and trigger/initiate the change towards clean project metadata in projects we depend on.

## Summary

This project already declares a valid SPDX license id/expression in its packaging metadata (`License: Apache-2.0` in the built METADATA), but the deprecated classifier `License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License` is still present. That classifier has no version and [PEP 639](https://peps.python.org/pep-0639/)-aware SBOM tooling like [cyclonedx-bom](https://pypi.org/project/cyclonedx-bom/) can't map it to an SPDX id, so it falls back to emitting the raw classifier text as a free-text license name. This free-text field is just noise and causes downstream tooling to flag this project as non-SPDX-compliant.

## Suggested fix

Remove the redundant `License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License` from `classifiers` in the packaging config. No change to the `license` field is needed.

## How to reproduce

```bash
uv tool install cyclonedx-bom
uv venv .venv-repro
uv pip install --python .venv-repro/bin/python requests
cyclonedx-py environment .venv-repro -o sbom.cdx.json
```

... and then check the `.licenses` property of the component. There should only something like:

```json
// This is how it should look like
...
    "license": {
        "acknowledgement": "declared",
        "id": "<VALID SPDX IDENTIFIER>"
    }
...
```

and _not_:

```json
// This is how it should not look like
...
    "license": {
       "acknowledgement": "declared",
       "name": "<CLASSIFIER TAKEN FROM METADATA"
    }
...
```

I'm happy to provide a PR to resolve this timely after approval!

This was discussed here multiple times in the past so I'm opening it as a public bug report.

`src/requests/utils.py`, `proxy_bypass_registry` (main, 2.34.2):

```python
if re.match(test, host, re.I):   # start-anchored only
    return True
```

re.match anchors only the start, so ProxyOverride=google.com matches google.com.evil.com and bypasses the proxy for it — an attacker-influenced hostname can escape a proxy meant to inspect traffic.

Diverges from CPython: this is a copy of CPython's old code. CPython now matches with fnmatch (anchored both ends, wildcards preserved). Verified on 3.14:
- `fnmatch("google.com.evil.com", "google.com")` → False (requests returns True)
- `fnmatch("a.example.net", "*.example.net")` → True

Fix: use fnmatch(host, test) to match CPython, or minimally anchor: re.match(test + r"\Z", host, re.I).

body_text:
## What happened

`# isort: split` on a **parenthesised** `from` import is not honoured on the pass that moves the import. The blank line the directive asks for only appears on the *next* run, and until then `isort --check` reports the file isort just wrote as needing changes.

```python
# repro.py
from zlib import (
    x,
) # isort: split
import os
```

```console
$ isort repro.py && cat repro.py && isort --check repro.py
import os
from zlib import x  # isort: split
Imports are incorrectly sorted and/or formatted.   # <- isort disagrees with isort
$ isort repro.py && cat repro.py && isort --check repro.py
import os

from zlib import x  # isort: split
$ isort --check repro.py   # clean, third run unchanged
```

So the sequence never converges in one step: a pre-commit hook or a CI `isort --check` sees a diff on a file that is already the output of `isort`.

This contradicts what `docs/configuration/action_comments.md` promises for the directive — "Tells isort the current sort section is finished, and all future imports belong to a new sort grouping" — and it breaks the invariant `tests/integration/test_hypothesmith.py::test_isort_is_idempotent` asserts.

## Exact trigger

I bisected the boundary. **Unstable** — directive plus parens plus a move:

| Input | First pass | Second pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `from zlib import (\n    x,\n) # isort: split\nimport os\n` | `import os\nfrom zlib import x  # isort: split\n` | adds a blank line |
| `from zlib import (\n    x,\n    y,\n) # isort: split\nimport os\n` | `import os\nfrom zlib import x, y  # isort: split\n` | adds a blank line |
| `from zlib import (  # isort: split\n    x,\n)\nimport os\n` | same as row 1 | adds a blank line |
| `from zlib import (\n    x,  # isort: split\n)\nimport os\n` | same as row 1 | adds a blank line |
| `import os\nimport abc\nfrom zlib import (\n    x,\n) # isort: split\n` | `import abc\nimport os\nfrom zlib import x  # isort: split\n` | adds a blank line |
| `from zlib import (\n    x,\n) # isort: split\nfrom abc import y\n` | `from abc import y\nfrom zlib import x  # isort: split\n` | adds a blank line |

<details><summary>What is stable, and where I think it goes wrong</summary>

**Stable** — every one of these is left alone, so the parens plus the move are both required:

- the same paren import with **no** directive, or with a plain `# note` comment, or with `# noqa`
- the directive **without** parens: `from zlib import x  # isort: split\nimport os\n`
- the directive **without** a move: `from zlib import (\n    x,\n) # isort: split\n` on its own
- the directive on a straight import that moves: `import zlib  # isort: split\nimport os\n`
- `force_sort_within_sections=True`, which has the same two-pass behaviour

## What happened

`isort` turns a valid Python file into one that cannot be parsed, and then reports that file as correctly sorted. No action comment and no non-default setting is involved.

```python
# repro.py — valid Python
from pkg.mod import (
    y,
); import os
```

```console
$ python -c "import ast; ast.parse(open('repro.py').read()); print('parses')"
parses
$ isort repro.py; echo "exit $?"
exit 0
$ cat repro.py
from pkg.mod import ;, import, os, y
$ python -c "import ast; ast.parse(open('repro.py').read())"
  File "repro.py", line 1
    from pkg.mod import ;, import, os, y
                             ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax
$ isort --check repro.py; echo "exit $?"
exit 0
```

The tokens of the statement after the `;` — `import`, `os` — are absorbed into the first import's list of names, along with the `;` itself. `import` and `from` end up where a module name belongs, which is why the result no longer parses. And because `isort --check` exits 0 on the corrupted file, a CI job that only runs `isort --check` will pass with the repository already broken.

## Scope

All of these take a valid input to an unparseable output, on `main` at `13758cf` with default settings:

| Input | isort output | parses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `from pkg.mod import (\n    y,\n); import os\n` | `from pkg.mod import ;, import, os, y\n` | no |
| `from pkg.mod import (\n    y,\n); from os import beta\n` | `from pkg.mod import ;, beta, from, import, os, y\n` | no |
| `from pkg.mod import (\n    y,\n); print(1)\n` | `from pkg.mod import 1, ;, print, y\n` | no |
| `from pkg.mod import (\n    y,\n    x,\n); import os\n` | `from pkg.mod import ;, import, os, x, y\n` | no |
| `import zlib\nfrom pkg.mod import (\n    y,\n); import os\n` | `import zlib\n\nfrom pkg.mod import ;, import, os, y\n` | no |
| `from pkg.mod import (\n    y,\n); import os  # note\n` | `from pkg.mod import ;, import, os, y  # note\n` | no |

<details><summary>Controls, and where I think it goes wrong</summary>

Controls, which behave correctly, so the trigger is narrow:

- `from pkg.mod import y; import os\n` — a `from` import **without** parentheses is split correctly into `import os\n\nfrom pkg.mod import y\n`
- `import os; from pkg.mod import (\n    y,\n)\n` — the parentheses are harmless when nothing follows the `;` on that logical line
- the same shapes with `;` inside a function body or after a `try:` are unaffected, because isort only rewrites the import block

</details>

## Where I think it goes wrong

`isort/parse.py` splits a physical line on `;` and then treats each piece as a statement:

```python
line, *end_of_line_comment = line.split("#", 1)
if ";" in line and not line[0].isspace():
    statements = [line.strip() for line in line.split(";")]
```

The first piece here is `from pkg.mod import (\n    y,\n` — the parenthesis is still open, so the import's *names* are not in that piece at all. The continuation lines (`    y,` and `)`) are read as separate physical lines, and by the time the `)` line is reached the `;`-split has already been decided for the first line. What the sorter then receives as the import's name list is the joined remainder, which is where `;`, `import` and `os` come from. I have not traced the import-collection path that turns those pieces into a name list, so treat the last step as inference; the split above is where I would start looking, and it is the same statement-splitting that #2674 and #2673 are about.

## How I found it

Property hunting on the two invariants a formatter must not break — `code(code(x)) == code(x)` and `check_code(code(x))` — over generated sources across ten configurations. This surfaced as a non-idempotence whose second pass differed only by a blank line, which is what made me look at the first pass with `ast.parse` instead of by eye. `ast.parse` is the check I would add to the property test: it is the only one of the three that says the output is unusable.

## Suggested next step

`tests/unit/test_regressions.py` is the natural home for a pinned case, and if the intent is to stop this class rather than these instances, an `ast.parse(isort.code(source))` assertion in `tests/integration/test_hypothesmith.py` would cover it. I am not opening a PR unprompted: the `;`-splitting code is shared with #2673 and #2674, and the right shape of the fix depends on whether a `;` inside an open parenthesis is meant to end the statement at all. Happy to send a PR with a regression test once that is settled — I would rather not guess at the semantics.

`tests/unit/test_regressions.py` is the natural home for a pinned case, and if the intent is to stop this class rather than these instances, an `ast.parse(isort.code(source))` assertion in `tests/integration/test_hypothesmith.py` would cover it. I am not opening a PR unprompted: the `;`-splitting code is shared with #2673 and #2674, and the right shape of the fix depends on whether a `;` inside an open parenthesis is meant to end the statement at all. Happy to send a PR with a regression test once that is settled — I would rather not guess at the semantics.

**isort rewrites the file on every run when an imported name carries its own inline comment** (shipped `black` profile, i.e. `multi_line_output=3`/`5`)

### Repro

```python
import isort

source = (
    "from pkg.submodule.submodule.submodule.submodule import (\n"
    "    alpha,  # type: ignore[import-untyped]\n"
    "    beta, gamma\n"
    ")\n"
)
first = isort.code(source, profile="black")
second = isort.code(first, profile="black")
assert first == second   # fails
```

The first pass gives `alpha` an import statement of its own, because that is the normal handling for a name with its own comment. But the one-name statement is then too long to fit, so `wrap.line()` hoists the comment onto the `from X import (` opening line:

```python
from pkg.submodule.submodule.submodule.submodule import (  # type: ignore[import-untyped]
    alpha
)
from pkg.submodule.submodule.submodule.submodule import beta, gamma
```

That opening-paren position is a *statement-level* position. On the next run isort reads the comment back as a comment for the whole import rather than for `alpha`, regroups the names, and rewrites the file again:

```python
from pkg.submodule.submodule.submodule.submodule import (  # type: ignore[import-untyped]
    alpha,
    beta,
    gamma
)
```

which is stable. So it settles after two passes, but in the meantime `isort --check` rejects isort's own output, and the file churns in version control — every run that touches the file produces a diff.

This needs a `line_length` short enough that `from <module> import <name>  # <comment>` does not fit, which is the normal case for a deeply-dotted module path. It affects any comment text, not only `# noqa`.

### Scope measured

<details>
<summary>Scope measured: 54 cases swept</summary>

I swept 54 cases (9 source shapes x `multi_line_output` 0-5, one process per case so no state leaks between them). On `9f905615`, 7 of the 54 are not idempotent:

| case | `multi_line_output=3` | `=5` |
|---|---|---|
| one name with a comment | churns | churns |
| two names with comments | churns | churns |
| three names with comments | churns | churns |
| comment on a name in the middle | stable | stable |

</details>

The middle case also does not converge after two passes under `multi_line_output=1` — a separate instance that I have not diagnosed.

### Root cause

`isort/output.py::_with_from_imports_for_module` splits a name carrying its own comment onto a statement of its own without accounting for `wrap.line()` subsequently hoisting that comment to the opening parenthesis in the vertical wrap modes. The function already has the guard for `multi_line_output=2`:

```python
            if (
                comment.lower().startswith("noqa")
                and config.multi_line_output == wrap_modes.WrapModes.HANGING_INDENT
            ):
                comments = list(comments) if comments else []
                comments.append(comment)
                continue
```

The comment preceding it — *"keep the name in the main list and hoist the comment to the statement"* — describes exactly the right treatment; it is just not applied to `VERTICAL_HANGING_INDENT` and `VERTICAL_GRID_GROUPED`, which hoist to the same `(` line via `wrap._hoist_comment_to_paren`.

`fee6e8ea` ("Fix output of hanging indent for long lines with noqa") added the mode-2 version; the vertical modes were not covered.

### Suggested fix, and where I think the real one is

The narrow fix is to extend the existing guard to the two vertical modes, hoisting the comment ourselves and keeping the name in the group. That is one `if` plus a length check, and it works because the hoisted position is the same position the buggy path was already producing — so the fix converges to isort's own fixed point, one pass earlier, rather than inventing new output.

The broader problem is that `wrap.line()` hoists a *name-level* comment to a *statement-level* position at all, which makes this class of bug recur: #2556, #2474 and #2491 are all adjacent fixes in the same area. A fix at that seam would be more general but larger, and I think it is a maintainer call whether to take it now or separately.

I would also flag the three-comments case as a distinct problem: those converge by joining the comments onto one line with `;`, which is stable but reads oddly and loses the association between comment and name. I do not have a fix for that and this report does not claim one.

body_text:
Across our ["SciTools repositories"](https://github.com/orgs/SciTools/repositories) we are running pre-commit autoupdates in GHA.
We keep hitting a problem where this attempts to update the isort version to an alpha or beta release, instead of a bona-fide stable version.
E.G. like [this](https://github.com/SciTools/ncdata/pull/269) .

I don't think we get this with other repos, and I assume this is because other packages don't publish their pre-releases in the same way.
The author of pre-commit [declined to address this](https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit/issues/995), because he chooses that pre-commit should not handle the semantic content of version strings.

Is there any way of fixing this ?

### Discussed in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/discussions/2980
Originally posted by **al-dpopowich** July 13, 2021 I have not been able to find this in a Discussion or Issue... If I have a python Enum: ```python import enum class StateAbbrev(enum.Enum): """State Abbreviations""" NY = "New York" MA = "Massachusetts" # etc ``` I can use this with SQLAlchemy... ```python from sqlalchemy import Table, Column, Enum # etc User = Table( 'myuser', ... Column('state', Enum(StateAbbrev)) ... ) ``` On saving, sqlalchemy uses *name* **NOT** the *value*. That is, sqlalchemy will store "NY", not "New York". Similarly, via my REST API, I want to accept the "codes" not the (possibly) long strings. This is a disconnect from pydantic which validates by value. I have seen answers to similar questions on stackoverflow suggest using the same value as name, e.g: ```python class Foo(enum.Enum): A = "A" B = "B" ``` But this is not practical when you want to offer your Enum as a CODE=>HUMAN_READABLE mapping. In short, what I want is a Config option, e.g., `validate_enum_by_name` (for backward compatibility, default to `False`): ```python # in validators.py def enum_member_validator(v: Any, field: 'ModelField', config: 'BaseConfig') -> Enum: enum = field.type_ try: enum_v = enum[v] if config.validate_enum_by_name else enum(v) except (KeyError, ValueError): # enum should be an enum, so will be iterable raise errors.EnumMemberError(enum_values=list(enum)) return enum_v.value if config.use_enum_values else enum_v ```

Using `"format": "binary"` for the JSON Schema of `bytes` comes from OpenAPI 3.0.x: https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.0.3.html#considerations-for-file-uploads.

Instead, we should make use of `contentEncoding` and `contentMediaType` (https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/draft-bhutton-json-schema-validation-01#section-8.3).

As `bytes` is a really common type, changing this in V2 would be quite disruptive.

See https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/12841. Rebased branch: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/tree/vp/bytes-contentencoding.

### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

**TL;DR**: `Field(exclude_if=...)` (added in 2.12, #12141) decides exclusion from the field
*value* alone. Some exclusion decisions depend on the *caller* instead — most notably: *omit
credential fields from every dump by default, include them only when persistence explicitly
opts in via `context`*. #12056 already sketches extending `exclude_if` with the serialization
context; this issue is a concrete, production-tested use case for that extension — and I would
happily try to implement it (including the `pydantic-core` side), in whichever shape you
prefer.

#### The use case

Models holding third-party credentials (`client_secret`, RSA keys, connection strings):

1. Every ordinary serialization — API response, log payload, anything fed to an LLM — must not
   contain these fields. Omitted entirely, not masked: nothing to leak, and nothing for an API
   client to echo back on `PUT`.
2. Exactly one caller (database persistence) needs the real values through the same
   `model_dump` path, and opts in explicitly:
   `model_dump(context={'include_secrets': True})`.

This is, in essence, the user-defined ser/val modes idea (`'api'` vs `'dump-to-db'`) floated
in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/12056#issuecomment-3191434441 — expressed with
the `context` mechanism that exists today.

#### Why the current tools don't cover it

- `Field(exclude=True)` — unconditional; persistence cannot opt back in.
- `Field(exclude_if=...)` — the callable receives only the value, and the decision here
  depends on the caller, not on the value. Trying to accept `info` fails:

  ```python

### Initial Checks - [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything - [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/) and still think this feature is missing ### Description Hi, guys! I really love pydantic, but there is the following issue that i really want to see resolved and i hope i can help: TL;DR: should `model_construct(...)` be typed (similar to `__init__`) and if so, what do you think about my solution of "copying" the `__init__` method signature? (If not, is there any official way of instantiating a model with type-checking but without validation?) Consider this simple model: ```python class User(BaseModel): id: int = Field(default_factory=lambda: randint(1, 1000)) name: str ``` If one wants to create model instances with data where the types are known at type-check time, they have to choose either `User(id=7, name="John Doe")` or `User.model_construct(id=7, name="John Doe")` The issue for me is, that the first option performs redundant (assuming type-checker correctness) validation at runtime and the second cannot perform any type-checks, because the signature is currently `model_construct(**kwargs: Any)`. According to your [docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/integrations/dev-tools/mypy/#generate-a-typed-signature-for-model_construct), the mypy plugin enables this behaviour for mypy, but a lot of users rely on other type-checking tools and it would be great if this functionality could be supported for them as well. Here is a simple (purely types-based) solution i came up with that seems to work for this use-case and i wanted to get some feedback before making it a proper MR. Essentially it simply copies the ParamSpec of the `__init__(...)` function into the `model_construct` method: ```python from typing_extensions import Protocol, TypeVar, ParamSpec, Callable, TYPE_CHECKING from pydantic import BaseModel P = ParamSpec("P") T = TypeVar("T") class model_construct_decorator: def __init__(self, f): pass def __get__(self, instance: None, owner: Callable[P, T]) -> Callable[P, T]: return owner class User(BaseModel): id: int = Field(default_factory=lambda: randint(1, 1000)) name: str if TYPE_CHECKING: @model_construct_decorator def model_construct_typed(self): ... else: @classmethod def model_construct_typed(cls, *args, **kwargs): return cls.model_construct(*args, **kwargs) User.model_construct_typed(id="7") # -> now also shows a type error in pyright ``` (The idea would be that what i currently named `model_construct_typed(...)` would be implemented as `model_construct(...)` on `BaseModel`) --- Now there are multiple solvable issues that ive left out for brevity, but here are their solutions for anyone interested:
1. What about the _fields_set argument of the current model_construct(...)? The `model_construct_decorator` can be updated as follows to reestablish that argument: ```python class ModelConstructCallable(Protocol[P, T]): def __call__(self, _fields_set: set[str]|None=None, *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> T: ... class model_construct_decorator: def __init__(self, f): pass def __get__(self, instance: None, owner: Callable[P, T]) -> ModelConstructCallable[P, T]: return lambda _fields_set=None, *args, **kwargs: owner(*args, **kwargs) # could also be a simple pass statement with type-ignore comment, because this should never actually be executed ```
2. Will any of the current type-checking behaviour break? Since users currently have the `**kwarg` option available, this switch may break their existing code, especially if the pass `extra` data to model construct, as now their type-checker will complain about the extra data. There are two solutions for that issue: a) either keep the `model_construct(...)` as is and add a new `model_construct_typed(...)` b) add a new argument (e.g. `_type_check: bool=False`, after `_fields_set`) that optionally enables this behaviour Here is an example implementation of solution b) from a type-checking perspective (at runtime there should be no difference): ```python class ModelConstructCallable(Protocol[P, T]): @overload def __call__(self, _fields_set: set[str]|None=None, _type_check: Literal[False]=False, **kwargs: Any) -> T: ... @overload def __call__(self, _fields_set: set[str]|None=None, _type_check: Literal[True], *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> T: ... class model_construct_decorator: def __init__(self, f): pass def __get__(self, instance: None, owner: Callable[P, T]) -> ModelConstructCallable[P, T]: return lambda _fields_set=None, _type_check=False, *args, **kwargs: owner(*args, **kwargs) # could also be a simple pass statement with type-ignore comment, because this should never actually be executed ... User.model_construct(id="7", some_extra_value=...) # still no type error as before User.model_construct(_type_check=True, id="7", some_extra_value="...") # type error as intended ```
3. What about the instance version of the current model_construct(...)? ### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Hello. According to the OpenAPI 3.1 spec, strict integer parsing should be relaxed.

https://swagger.io/specification/v3.1/

> Since there is no distinct JSON integer type, JSON Schema defines integers mathematically. This means that both 1 and 1.0 are [equivalent](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-bhutton-json-schema-00#section-4.2.2), and are both considered to be integers.

So, to comply with the specification, we should accept values like `2.0` when the fractional part is `0` and treat them as integers even when `strict=True` is enabled.

### Example Code

```Python
import pydantic


class MyModel(pydantic.BaseModel):
    value: int = pydantic.Field(strict=True)


print(MyModel.model_validate({'value': 2.0}))
```

### Description

Hello. According to the OpenAPI 3.1 spec, strict integer parsing should be relaxed.

https://swagger.io/specification/v3.1/

> Since there is no distinct JSON integer type, JSON Schema defines integers mathematically. This means that both 1 and 1.0 are [equivalent](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-bhutton-json-schema-00#section-4.2.2), and are both considered to be integers.

So, to comply with the specification, we should accept values like `2.0` when the fractional part is `0` and treat them as integers even when `strict=True` is enabled.

### Example Code

```Python
import pydantic


class MyModel(pydantic.BaseModel):
    value: int = pydantic.Field(strict=True)


print(MyModel.model_validate({'value': 2.0}))
```

As `model_construct()` bypasses validation, it doesn't try to rebuild the model first if it is incomplete. This could cause issues with serialization inference (fixed differently in https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/13922), but also when using referring to `FieldInfo` attributes such as `alias`, as per this failing test:

https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/5c2a929726717b9a98575e245a180a082f1b7d26/tests/test_construction.py#L674-L694

As such, we should try to rebuild the model before using `model_construct()` (only doable in v3).
